Python Mastery

Everything between "I can write Python" and "I can be trusted with Python in production." The object model that explains the language's behaviour, the type system professionals actually run in CI, concurrency in all four of its Python flavours, the tooling that ships code to PyPI, and the ecosystem you will be expected to know.

How to use this course

  • This course assumes you can already write Python. Loops, functions, classes, lists and dictionaries should be familiar. If they are not, work through the Foundations course first — this one starts where that one stops.
  • Everything here targets Python 3.14 (released October 2025, supported to October 2030). Where a feature is newer than 3.10, the version that introduced it is stated inline, because you will be reading code written for older interpreters for years to come.
  • Run every example. Python is an unusually honest language: almost every claim in this course can be confirmed in a REPL in under ten seconds, and the ones that surprise you are the ones worth confirming. Every output block below was produced by actually running the code above it.
  • Each section is Concept → Mechanism → Practice → Exercises with solutions. The mechanism matters: most Python confusion is a correct mental model applied to the wrong layer.
  • Set yourself up before section 1:
python3 --version          # 3.14 or newer for the whole course
mkdir ~/python-mastery && cd ~/python-mastery
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate

Versions every output block in this course was produced against: Python 3.14.4 · pytest 9.1.1, on Linux.

What you are actually learning

Not a tour of features. Five layers, each of which explains a class of behaviour that otherwise looks arbitrary:

  1. The object model. Names bind to objects, everything is an object, and attribute lookup follows the method resolution order through descriptors. Mutable defaults, identity against equality, and why += on a tuple member both fails and succeeds all fall out of those rules (§1).
  2. The protocols the language calls for you. Special methods make your objects work with len, in, with, indexing and the operators; dataclasses, __slots__, abstract base classes and protocols say what a class is and what it requires (§2–§3).
  3. Types a checker enforces. Protocols, generics, variance, TypedDict, overloads and narrowing — run in CI, and applied where they earn their keep rather than everywhere (§6).
  4. Concurrency matched to the workload. Threads, processes, the free-threaded build, subinterpreters and asyncio are answers to different bottlenecks, and the wrong one is slower than none (§8–§9).
  5. Shipping. An installable project with a lockfile, tests that fail when the code is wrong, a linter and a formatter that run automatically, and a package with an entry point (§11–§12).

By the end you should be able to read an ordinary Python codebase without finding any part of it opaque, and to make the choices — class design, types, concurrency, packaging — that decide whether it can be trusted in production.

SECTION 1

The Object Model

Python has a reputation for being simple. It is not simple — it is consistent. Almost everything that surprises people about Python is a consequence of one small set of rules about what objects are, how names refer to them, and how attributes are found. Learn those rules once and a very large amount of Python stops needing to be memorised.

This section is the foundation the rest of the course stands on. It is deliberately the densest section here.

1.1 The Data Model Is the Language

The data model is Python's specification of what an object is and how the interpreter interacts with it. It is the reason len(x), x + y, for i in x and with x: work on your own classes exactly as they work on built-in ones: each of those syntaxes is defined as a call to a named method, and any object providing that method participates.

That is the central design decision of the language. Other languages special-case their built-in types and offer user types a lesser status. Python defines the built-ins in terms of the same protocol it offers you. list is not privileged; it simply implements __len__, __getitem__, __iter__ and the rest.

Three properties belong to every object, and only the third can ever change:

Property What it is Changes?
Identity Its address in memory, returned by id() Never
Type The class that defines its behaviour, returned by type() Effectively never
Value The data it holds Only if the type is mutable 
x = [1, 2, 3]
print(id(x) == id(x))       # identity is stable
print(type(x).__name__)     # type is fixed
x.append(4)                 # value can change...
print(x, id(x) == id(x))    # ...without the identity changing

True
list
[1, 2, 3, 4] True

An object's identity is fixed for its whole lifetime, which is what makes is meaningful and what makes mutation visible through every name that refers to the object.

1.2 Names Are Not Boxes

The single most valuable correction to make to a self-taught mental model is this: a Python variable is not a box that holds a value. It is a name bound to an object. Assignment never copies, and never mutates. It only rebinds.

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a                # b is a second name for the SAME list
b.append(4)          # mutating through one name...
print(a)             # ...is visible through the other
b = [9, 9]           # rebinding b does NOT touch the list a refers to
print(a)

[1, 2, 3, 4]
[1, 2, 3, 4]
a
⟶
list object [1, 2, 3, 4]  id 0x7f…a10
b
⟶
↑ the same object, until b = [9, 9] rebinds it elsewhere

This one rule explains the classic surprises:

def add_item(items=[]):          # DANGER: evaluated ONCE, at def time
    items.append('x')
    return items

print(add_item())
print(add_item())                # the same list, still holding the first 'x'

['x']
['x', 'x']

The default value is an object created when the def statement runs, bound into the function object, and reused on every call that does not supply an argument. It is not re-created per call. The fix is the standard sentinel idiom:

def add_item(items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append('x')
    return items

print(add_item(), add_item())

['x'] ['x']

Function arguments follow the same rule. Python is neither "pass by value" nor "pass by reference" in the C++ sense; it passes the object, bound to a new local name. Mutating the object is visible to the caller; rebinding the local name is not.

def mutate(lst, num):
    lst.append(99)      # mutation — caller sees it
    num += 1            # rebinding a local name — caller does not
    return num

data, n = [1], 5
mutate(data, n)
print(data, n)

[1, 99] 5

1.3 The Standard Type Hierarchy

The Language Reference organises every built-in type into a hierarchy worth knowing, because a surprising number of "why does this work?" questions are answered by "because it is in that group."

  • None, NotImplemented, Ellipsis — singletons. None is the sole instance of NoneType; that is why x is None is both correct and fast. NotImplemented is what a binary operator returns to say "I don't handle this type, try the other operand's method." Ellipsis (...) is a real object, used heavily by NumPy slicing and as a placeholder body.
  • Numbers — int (arbitrary precision), float (C double), complex, and the separate Fraction/Decimal types. bool is a subclass of int, which is why True + True == 2 and why isinstance(True, int) is True.
  • Sequences — immutable (str, bytes, tuple, range) and mutable (list, bytearray).
  • Set types — set (mutable) and frozenset (hashable, so it can be a dict key).
  • Mappings — dict, plus types.MappingProxyType for a read-only view.
  • Callables — functions, methods, classes, and any instance with __call__.
  • Modules, classes, instances, exceptions — all ordinary objects with dictionaries you can inspect.
print(isinstance(True, int), True + True)
print(type(...), type(NotImplemented))

True 2
<class 'ellipsis'> <class 'NotImplementedType'>

1.4 Identity, Equality and Interning

== asks the objects whether they consider themselves equal (it calls __eq__). is asks whether they are literally the same object. They are different questions and they are not interchangeable.

a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
print(a == b, a is b)

True False

Where this gets confusing is interning: CPython reuses certain immutable objects instead of creating new ones, as an optimisation. Small integers from −5 to 256 are pre-created at startup, and many string literals are cached.

a, b = 256, 256
print(a is b)
c, d = 257, 257          # module-level constants folded by the compiler
print(c is d)
e = int('257'); f = int('257')   # built at runtime — genuinely distinct
print(e is f, e == f)

True
True
False True

Note what happened in the middle case: 257 is 257 came out True not because 257 is interned, but because the compiler folded both literals in the same code object into one constant. Build the values at runtime and the illusion disappears. This is exactly why the rule is absolute:

Use is only for singletons — None, True, False, and sentinels you created yourself. Use == for values. Interning is a CPython implementation detail, it differs between versions and interpreters, and code that depends on it is broken code that happens to work.

Python 3.8 and later emit a SyntaxWarning when you compare a literal with is, precisely because it is so reliably a bug.

The idiomatic sentinel, when None is a legitimate value you must distinguish from "not supplied":

_MISSING = object()          # unique, falsy-free, cheap

def get(cfg, key, default=_MISSING):
    if key in cfg:
        return cfg[key]
    if default is _MISSING:
        raise KeyError(key)
    return default

print(get({'a': 1}, 'a'), get({}, 'b', None))

1 None

1.5 Mutability, Hashing and the Contract Between Them

An object is hashable if it has a __hash__ that stays constant for its lifetime and an __eq__ consistent with it. Dictionaries and sets require hashable keys, because they locate entries by hash bucket. Mutable built-ins deliberately set __hash__ = None.

try:
    {[1, 2]: 'nope'}
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)
print(hash((1, 2)) == hash((1, 2)))

TypeError: cannot use 'list' as a dict key (unhashable type: 'list')
True

(That precise wording is a Python 3.14 improvement — earlier versions said only unhashable type: 'list', leaving you to work out where the unhashable value was being used. The bare form is still what hash() itself raises.)

The contract is: equal objects must have equal hashes. The reverse is not required (different objects may collide). Break the forward direction and dictionaries silently misbehave — you insert a key and cannot find it again. This is why defining __eq__ on a class sets __hash__ to None automatically unless you define it too; Python would rather make your class unhashable than let it corrupt a dict. Section 2 covers how to do this correctly.

A tuple is only hashable if everything inside it is:

print(hash(('a', 1)) is not None)
try:
    hash(('a', [1]))
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

True
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'

1.6 How Attribute Lookup Actually Works

obj.attr looks like a field access. It is a method call — type(obj).__getattribute__(obj, 'attr') — and the default implementation follows a specific, learnable order:

1. Look in type(obj) and its MRO for a data descriptor (defines __set__ or __delete__) — if found, call its __get__ and stop.
2. Look in obj.__dict__ — if found, return it and stop.
3. Look in the type's MRO again for a non-data descriptor (only __get__, e.g. a plain function) or a plain class attribute.
4. Fall back to type(obj).__getattr__(obj, 'attr') if the class defines one; otherwise raise AttributeError.

Two consequences follow immediately, and both come up constantly in real code.

Class attributes are shared until shadowed. Assigning to self.x writes into the instance dictionary, hiding the class attribute rather than changing it:

class Counter:
    total = 0                 # one object, shared by all instances

a, b = Counter(), Counter()
a.total += 1                  # reads class attr 0, writes INSTANCE attr 1
print(a.total, b.total, Counter.total)
print(a.__dict__, b.__dict__)

1 0 0
{'total': 1} {}

If the class attribute is mutable, there is no rebinding, so nothing gets shadowed and every instance shares one object — the class-level version of the mutable-default bug:

class Basket:
    items = []                # shared by every Basket ever made

x, y = Basket(), Basket()
x.items.append('apple')
print(y.items)

['apple']

__getattr__ is a fallback, not a hook. It runs only when normal lookup has already failed, which makes it cheap and safe for proxies and lazy loading. __getattribute__ runs on every access and is very easy to make infinitely recursive:

class Config:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self._data = data
    def __getattr__(self, name):          # only called on failure
        try:
            return self._data[name]
        except KeyError:
            raise AttributeError(name) from None

c = Config({'host': 'localhost'})
print(c.host)
try:
    c.port
except AttributeError as exc:
    print('AttributeError:', exc)

localhost
AttributeError: port

Raising AttributeError — not KeyError — is required, because hasattr(), getattr(obj, n, default) and copy/pickle all probe with attribute access and expect that specific exception.

1.7 __slots__ and the Cost of a Dictionary

Every ordinary instance carries a __dict__, which is what makes Python objects so flexible: you can attach an attribute that the class never declared. That flexibility has a memory price, and for objects you create by the million it is the dominant cost.

__slots__ tells the class to allocate a fixed array of attribute descriptors instead of a dictionary:

import sys

class PointDict:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

class PointSlots:
    __slots__ = ('x', 'y')
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

d, s = PointDict(1, 2), PointSlots(1, 2)
print('dict version has __dict__:', hasattr(d, '__dict__'))
print('slots version has __dict__:', hasattr(s, '__dict__'))
d.z = 3                    # fine — arbitrary attributes allowed
try:
    s.z = 3
except AttributeError as exc:
    print('AttributeError:', exc)
print('slot descriptor:', type(PointSlots.x).__name__)

dict version has __dict__: True
slots version has __dict__: False
AttributeError: 'PointSlots' object has no attribute 'z' and no __dict__ for setting new attributes
slot descriptor: member_descriptor

Note the last line: __slots__ is implemented with descriptors, the mechanism section 3 covers in full. The entries are not magic strings — they become class-level objects that know how to read and write a fixed offset.

Practical rules:

  • The saving is real but not free: you lose dynamic attributes, and you must repeat __slots__ in subclasses (a subclass without it regains a __dict__, undoing the benefit).
  • Multiple inheritance from two classes that both define non-empty __slots__ is an error.
  • Reach for it when profiling says instance memory matters, not by default. dataclasses supports @dataclass(slots=True) since Python 3.10, which is the ergonomic way to get it.

1.8 Reference Counting

CPython reclaims memory primarily by reference counting: every object records how many references point at it, and when that count reaches zero the object is freed immediately and deterministically.

import sys

class Noisy:
    def __del__(self):
        print('freed')

n = Noisy()
m = n                        # count goes up
del n                        # ...down; still one reference left
print('still alive')
del m                        # count hits zero -> freed right here
print('after')

still alive
freed
after

That determinism is a genuine feature — it is why open(...) without a with block usually still closes the file, and why CPython needs no explicit free. Two cautions:

  • sys.getrefcount() always reports one extra, because passing the object to the function creates a temporary reference.
  • It is a CPython implementation detail. PyPy and the free-threaded build (section 8) do not promise prompt destruction. Never rely on __del__ running at a particular moment; use a context manager, which section 2 covers, when cleanup timing matters.

1.9 Cycles and the Garbage Collector

Reference counting alone cannot free a cycle: two objects that refer to each other never reach zero, even when nothing outside can reach them. CPython therefore also runs a second mechanism: generational garbage collection, a collector that periodically finds unreachable cycles and reclaims them.

import gc

class Node:
    def __init__(self):
        self.other = None

gc.collect()                      # start from a clean slate
a, b = Node(), Node()
a.other, b.other = b, a           # a cycle: each holds the other
del a, b                          # refcounts are 1, not 0 -> leaked so far
print('collected by cycle GC:', gc.collect() > 0)

collected by cycle GC: True

"Generational" garbage collection means objects are tracked in three generations; survivors are promoted, and older generations are scanned less often, on the empirical observation that most objects die young. gc.get_threshold() shows the allocation counts that trigger each generation.

You rarely need to touch the collector, but three interventions are legitimate and appear in real systems:

  • gc.freeze() after startup, before forking worker processes — it moves existing objects to a permanent generation so the collector does not touch them, keeping copy-on-write memory shared instead of dirtied.
  • gc.disable() in a short-lived batch process with a known allocation pattern, where you would rather spend memory than collector time.
  • gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_LEAK) when hunting an actual leak.

Containers are tracked; simple immutable objects like a plain int are not, because they cannot participate in a cycle:

import gc
print(gc.is_tracked([]), gc.is_tracked(1), gc.is_tracked('abc'))

True False False

1.10 Weak References

Sometimes you want to refer to an object without keeping it alive — a cache, an observer registry, a parent pointer that must not create a cycle. A weak reference does exactly that: it points at the object but does not raise its reference count.

import weakref

class Image:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

img = Image('cat.png')
ref = weakref.ref(img)
print(ref() is img)              # call it to dereference
del img
print(ref())                     # target is gone: the ref goes dead

True
None

weakref.WeakValueDictionary is the practical form: a cache whose entries vanish as soon as the rest of the program stops using them, so the cache never keeps an object alive on its own.

import weakref

class Session:
    def __init__(self, sid):
        self.sid = sid

cache = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()
s = Session('abc')
cache['abc'] = s
print(len(cache))
del s                            # the last strong reference
print(len(cache))

1
0

Two constraints worth knowing before you design around it: not every object can be weakly referenced — int, str, tuple and plain list/dict instances cannot, and a class using __slots__ cannot unless '__weakref__' is included in the slots. Use weakref.finalize() rather than __del__ when you need a cleanup callback, because it runs reliably at interpreter shutdown and does not resurrect the object.

import weakref

class Conn:
    __slots__ = ('name', '__weakref__')      # opt back in
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

c = Conn('db')
print(weakref.ref(c)() is c)

True

1.11 Looking at Objects From the Outside

Everything above is inspectable at runtime, which is one of Python's real advantages when debugging. The tools worth having at your fingertips:

import sys

class Widget:
    kind = 'ui'
    def __init__(self):
        self.label = 'ok'

w = Widget()
print(w.__dict__)                       # instance state only
print(Widget.__mro__)                   # resolution order (section 3)
print([k for k in vars(Widget) if not k.startswith('_')])   # class namespace
print(type(w) is Widget, isinstance(w, object))
print(sys.getsizeof(1), sys.getsizeof(2**64))

{'label': 'ok'}
(<class '__main__.Widget'>, <class 'object'>)
['kind']
True True
28 36

That last line is a nice demonstration that int is arbitrary-precision: a value too large for a machine word simply takes more bytes, with no overflow and no wraparound.

Exercises

Exercise 1.1 — Predict the output. Without running it, say what this prints and why.

def collect(value, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(value)
    return bucket

print(collect(1))
print(collect(2))
print(collect(3, []))
print(collect(4))
Solution 
[1]
[1, 2]
[3]
[1, 2, 4]

The default [] is created once, when the def statement executes, and stored on the function object. Calls 1, 2 and 4 all mutate that same list. Call 3 supplies its own list, so it is untouched by the others and does not affect the shared one. You can see the culprit directly:

def collect(value, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(value)
    return bucket

collect(1); collect(2)
print(collect.__defaults__)

([1, 2],)

Exercise 1.2 — Fix the shared-state bug. This class is supposed to give every robot its own log. Explain the bug and fix it.

class Robot:
    log = []
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def say(self, msg):
        self.log.append(f'{self.name}: {msg}')
Solution

log is a class attribute — one list shared by every instance. self.log.append(...) never rebinds self.log, so it never creates an instance attribute; it mutates the single shared list. Move the list into __init__ so each instance builds its own:

class Robot:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.log = []                # per instance
    def say(self, msg):
        self.log.append(f'{self.name}: {msg}')

a, b = Robot('R1'), Robot('R2')
a.say('hi')
print(a.log, b.log)

['R1: hi'] []

The general rule: a mutable class attribute is almost always a bug, because rebinding-shadows-but-mutation-shares. An immutable class attribute (kind = 'ui', MAX = 100) is fine and idiomatic.

Exercise 1.3 — Identity vs equality. Explain why the first comparison is True and the second is False, and say what you should have written instead.

a = 'hello'
b = 'hello'
print(a is b)

x = 'hello world!'
y = ''.join(['hello', ' ', 'world!'])
print(x is y)
Solution

Both print the same string value; only the object identity differs. 'hello' is a name-like literal, so CPython interns it at compile time and both names point at one cached object. The second string is built at runtime by join, producing a brand-new object that is never interned automatically.

The correct comparison in both cases is ==, which asks about value:

x = 'hello world!'
y = ''.join(['hello', ' ', 'world!'])
print(x == y, x is y)

True False

Interning is an optimisation, not a guarantee. It varies by CPython version, by whether the string looks like an identifier, and by whether the values sit in the same code object.

Exercise 1.4 — Attribute lookup order. Predict the output, then explain which step of the lookup algorithm produced each line.

class Base:
    greeting = 'class attribute'
    def __getattr__(self, name):
        return f'fallback for {name}'

b = Base()
print(b.greeting)
b.greeting = 'instance attribute'
print(b.greeting)
print(b.anything)
del b.greeting
print(b.greeting)
Solution 
class attribute
instance attribute
fallback for anything
class attribute

Line 1: nothing in the instance dict, so step 3 finds the plain class attribute. Line 2: the assignment put a key in b.__dict__, so step 2 wins and shadows the class. Line 3: neither the instance nor the class has anything, so normal lookup fails and step 4 calls __getattr__. Line 4: del removed the instance key, un-shadowing the class attribute — the class attribute was never modified, only hidden.

Note that __getattr__ was never consulted for greeting, on any line. It is a fallback that runs only after the normal search fails, which is exactly what makes it cheap.

Exercise 1.5 — Break a reference cycle with weakref. This parent/child pair leaks: the cycle keeps both objects alive until the cyclic collector happens to run. Rewrite the child's back-pointer so the pair is freed by reference counting alone.

class Parent:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = []
    def add(self, child):
        self.children.append(child)
        child.parent = self          # strong back-reference -> cycle

class Child:
    pass
Solution

Make the back-pointer weak. weakref.proxy is convenient here because it forwards attribute access, so calling code does not change:

import gc, weakref

class Parent:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.children = []
    def add(self, child):
        self.children.append(child)
        child.parent = weakref.proxy(self)

class Child:
    pass

gc.collect()
p = Parent('root')
p.add(Child())
print(p.children[0].parent.name)     # forwards like the real object
before = gc.collect()
del p
print('cycles collected on delete:', gc.collect())

root
cycles collected on delete: 0

The final 0 is the point: nothing was left for the cycle collector to do, because the only strong reference chain ran parent → children, and dropping p took the whole structure to zero immediately. With the original strong back-reference, that number is non-zero.

Use weakref.ref instead of proxy when you want explicit ref() calls and an obvious None when the target is gone; use proxy when you want transparent forwarding. Either way the parent must be kept alive by someone else — a weak reference is not ownership.

SECTION 2

Special Methods and Protocols

Section 1 said the data model is the language. This section is the proof: a tour of the special methods — the double-underscore, or dunder, methods — that every piece of Python syntax is defined in terms of.

The mental shift to make here is that dunder methods are not "magic" and you do not call them. You implement them, and the interpreter calls them on your behalf when the corresponding syntax appears. len(x) is defined as "call type(x).__len__(x)". Nothing more mysterious than that is happening.

2.1 Syntax Is a Protocol

A protocol in Python is an informal interface: a set of dunder methods that, if you implement them, make your object work with a piece of syntax or a built-in function. There is no implements keyword. If your class has __len__, len() works on it. That is the whole contract.

You write Python calls
len(x) type(x).__len__(x)
x[k] type(x).__getitem__(x, k)
x + y type(x).__add__(x, y), then type(y).__radd__(y, x)
for i in x type(x).__iter__(x), then __next__ repeatedly
with x: type(x).__enter__(x) … type(x).__exit__(x, …)
x(…) type(x).__call__(x, …)
if x: type(x).__bool__(x), else __len__, else True
repr(x) type(x).__repr__(x)

Note the left column of that table: lookup happens on the type, not the instance. This is the single most surprising rule about special methods, and it is deliberate — it lets the interpreter cache and optimise the lookup.

class Sneaky:
    pass

s = Sneaky()
s.__len__ = lambda: 42          # attaches to the INSTANCE, not the type
try:
    print(len(s))
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

Sneaky.__len__ = lambda self: 42   # on the type — now it works
print(len(s))

TypeError: object of type 'Sneaky' has no len()
42

2.2 Construction: __new__ and __init__

Creating an instance is two steps, not one. __new__ allocates and returns the object; __init__ initialises the object it is handed. type.__call__ runs both.

class Traced:
    def __new__(cls, *args):
        print('  __new__ called, args =', args)
        return super().__new__(cls)      # actually allocate
    def __init__(self, value):
        print('  __init__ called, value =', value)
        self.value = value

print('constructing:')
t = Traced(7)
print(t.value)

constructing:
  __new__ called, args = (7,)
  __init__ called, value = 7
7

You almost never need __new__. The exceptions are genuine and worth recognising:

  • Subclassing an immutable type. By the time __init__ runs, a str or tuple already has its value; there is nothing left to initialise, so customisation has to happen in __new__.
  • Caching or singletons — returning an existing instance instead of a fresh one.
class Upper(str):
    def __new__(cls, value):
        return super().__new__(cls, value.upper())

u = Upper('hello')
print(u, type(u).__name__, u.startswith('HE'))

HELLO Upper True

The rule that catches people: if __new__ returns an object that is not an instance of cls, __init__ is never called.

class Weird:
    def __new__(cls):
        return 'just a string'       # not a Weird
    def __init__(self):
        print('never runs')

print(repr(Weird()))

'just a string'

2.3 Representation: __repr__, __str__ and __format__

Two string conversions exist because they have two audiences.

  • __repr__ is for you — unambiguous, aimed at a developer reading a log or a REPL. The convention is that it should look like the expression that would rebuild the object.
  • __str__ is for the user — readable. It defaults to __repr__ if you do not define it, which is why __repr__ is the one to always write and __str__ is optional.
class Money:
    def __init__(self, amount, currency='GBP'):
        self.amount, self.currency = amount, currency
    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Money({self.amount!r}, {self.currency!r})'
    def __str__(self):
        return f'{self.amount:.2f} {self.currency}'
    def __format__(self, spec):
        if spec == 'short':
            return f'{self.currency}{self.amount:.0f}'
        return format(str(self), spec)

m = Money(12.5)
print(repr(m))
print(str(m))
print(f'{m}', f'{m:short}', f'{m:>12}')
print([m])                        # containers use repr of their elements

Money(12.5, 'GBP')
12.50 GBP
12.50 GBP GBP12    12.50 GBP
[Money(12.5, 'GBP')]

Three details in that example earn their keep. {m:short} prints GBP12, not GBP13, because format(12.5, '.0f') rounds half to even — the IEEE-754 default that Python uses everywhere, including the built-in round(). It is not a bug, and it is the reason money should be stored as Decimal or as integer minor units rather than as float. The !r conversion in the f-string calls repr() on the field, which is what makes the output round-trippable. And printing a list of objects shows their __repr__, never their __str__ — a container asks its elements for their unambiguous form. That is why a class with only __str__ produces the useless <__main__.Money object at 0x7f…> the moment you put it in a list.

2.4 Equality and Hashing, Done Correctly

Section 1 stated the contract: equal objects must hash equal. Here is how to satisfy it.

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y
    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Point({self.x}, {self.y})'
    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Point):
            return NotImplemented          # let the other side try
        return (self.x, self.y) == (other.x, other.y)
    def __hash__(self):
        return hash((self.x, self.y))      # same fields as __eq__

a, b = Point(1, 2), Point(1, 2)
print(a == b, a is b)
print(len({a, b}))                          # equal + equal hash -> one entry
print({a: 'origin-ish'}[b])                 # b finds a's entry

True False
1
origin-ish

Three rules make this work every time:

  1. Hash the same fields you compare, as a tuple. If __eq__ looks at x and y, __hash__ must too.
  2. Return NotImplemented, not False, for unknown types. False asserts inequality; NotImplemented tells Python to try the reflected operation on the other operand, and only then fall back to identity comparison. Returning False breaks comparisons against types that would have known how to compare with yours.
  3. Only hash immutable state. If x can change after the object goes into a set, the object's hash bucket becomes wrong and it is effectively lost.

Defining __eq__ sets __hash__ = None unless you also define __hash__, making the class unhashable:

class Mutable:
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return isinstance(other, Mutable) and self.v == other.v

print(Mutable.__hash__)
try:
    {Mutable(1)}
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

None
TypeError: cannot use 'Mutable' as a set element (unhashable type: 'Mutable')

That is Python protecting you, not obstructing you: a mutable object with value equality is genuinely unsafe as a dict key, so the default is to refuse.

2.5 Ordering

Six comparison dunders exist: __lt__, __le__, __gt__, __ge__, plus __eq__ and __ne__. Implementing all of them by hand is tedious and easy to get subtly wrong, so functools.total_ordering fills in the rest from __eq__ and one ordering method.

from functools import total_ordering

@total_ordering
class Version:
    def __init__(self, text):
        self.parts = tuple(int(p) for p in text.split('.'))
    def __repr__(self):
        return 'v' + '.'.join(map(str, self.parts))
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return isinstance(other, Version) and self.parts == other.parts
    def __lt__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Version):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.parts < other.parts

vs = [Version('1.10.0'), Version('1.2.0'), Version('1.9.3')]
print(sorted(vs))
print(Version('1.2.0') <= Version('1.9.3'))    # supplied by total_ordering
print(max(vs))

[v1.2.0, v1.9.3, v1.10.0]
True
v1.10.0

Note that this sorts 1.10.0 after 1.9.3, which string comparison would get backwards — the tuple of integers is doing the work. Sorting, min, max, heapq and bisect all need only __lt__; that is the one to define if you define just one.

2.6 Operator Overloading

Arithmetic operators map to dunders in a symmetrical, three-stage system that is worth understanding in full because it explains how 2 * vector can work when int has never heard of your class.

For x + y, Python tries:

  1. type(x).__add__(x, y)
  2. If that returned NotImplemented, type(y).__radd__(y, x) — the reflected operation
  3. If that also declined, raise TypeError
class Vec:
    def __init__(self, *xs):
        self.xs = tuple(xs)
    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Vec{self.xs}'
    def __add__(self, other):
        if isinstance(other, Vec):
            return Vec(*(a + b for a, b in zip(self.xs, other.xs)))
        return NotImplemented
    def __mul__(self, k):
        if isinstance(k, (int, float)):
            return Vec(*(a * k for a in self.xs))
        return NotImplemented
    __rmul__ = __mul__                      # scalar * vector == vector * scalar
    def __neg__(self):
        return self * -1

v, w = Vec(1, 2), Vec(10, 20)
print(v + w)
print(v * 3)
print(3 * v)          # int.__mul__(3, v) declines -> Vec.__rmul__ runs
print(-v)
try:
    v + 5
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

Vec(11, 22)
Vec(3, 6)
Vec(3, 6)
Vec(-1, -2)
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'Vec' and 'int'

That TypeError message is generated by the interpreter, not by you — it is what you get for free by returning NotImplemented instead of raising. Returning NotImplemented is how you say "not my job"; raising is how you say "nobody's job."

In-place operators (+=) try __iadd__ first and fall back to __add__ followed by a rebind. This is the difference between list and tuple under +=:

a = [1, 2]
before = id(a)
a += [3]                 # list.__iadd__ mutates in place
print(a, id(a) == before)

t = (1, 2)
before = id(t)
t += (3,)                # no __iadd__ -> builds a new tuple, rebinds t
print(t, id(t) == before)

[1, 2, 3] True
(1, 2, 3) False

The full operator set follows the same pattern throughout: __sub__/__rsub__/__isub__, __matmul__ for @ (used by NumPy), __truediv__ and __floordiv__, __mod__, __pow__, the bitwise family, and the unary __neg__, __pos__, __abs__, __invert__.

2.7 The Container Protocol

Four dunders make an object behave like a collection, and you can adopt as few as you need.

class Deck:
    def __init__(self, cards):
        self._cards = list(cards)
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self._cards)
    def __getitem__(self, key):
        return self._cards[key]              # slices work for free
    def __setitem__(self, key, value):
        self._cards[key] = value
    def __contains__(self, card):
        return card in self._cards

d = Deck(['A', 'K', 'Q', 'J'])
print(len(d), d[0], d[-1], d[1:3])
print('Q' in d)
d[0] = '10'
print(list(d))                                # iterable via __getitem__ alone
print(list(reversed(d)))                      # reversed() too

4 A J ['K', 'Q']
True
['10', 'K', 'Q', 'J']
['J', 'Q', 'K', '10']

The last two lines are the payoff for a design decision made long before __iter__ existed: if a class has __getitem__ accepting integers from 0 upward, Python falls back to calling it with 0, 1, 2… until IndexError, giving you iteration, in, reversed() and unpacking without writing another line. Section 5 covers __iter__, which is the modern and more efficient way to say the same thing.

One practical caveat, because it will bite you in a typed codebase: static type checkers do not model this fallback. Fully annotate the class above and mypy still rejects list(d) with "No overload variant of list matches argument type Deck", because Iterable is defined structurally as "has __iter__" and Deck does not. The code runs correctly; the checker is describing the modern protocol rather than the legacy one. If you want both the iteration and a clean type check, define __iter__ explicitly — which is the better habit anyway.

__contains__ is optional — without it, in falls back to a linear scan through iteration — but defining it lets you answer membership in better than O(n) when your data structure can.

2.8 Callables

Any object with __call__ can be called. This gives you a function with state, which is often clearer than a closure and always easier to introspect and pickle.

class RateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, limit):
        self.limit, self.count = limit, 0
    def __call__(self, request):
        self.count += 1
        if self.count > self.limit:
            return f'{request}: rejected'
        return f'{request}: allowed ({self.count}/{self.limit})'

allow = RateLimiter(2)
print(allow('GET /'), allow('GET /a'), allow('GET /b'), sep='\n')
print(callable(allow), callable(42))

GET /: allowed (1/2)
GET /a: allowed (2/2)
GET /b: rejected
True False

This is also why classes themselves are callable: type defines __call__, and calling a class is what triggers the __new__/__init__ pair from section 2.2.

2.9 The Context Manager Protocol

with is defined by exactly two methods. __enter__ runs on entry and its return value is bound by as; __exit__ runs on the way out — whether or not an exception occurred — which is what makes it the correct tool for any acquire/release pair.

class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        print('  acquiring')
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        print('  releasing; exception was', exc_type.__name__ if exc_type else None)
        return False                 # False/None -> propagate; True -> suppress

with Timer() as t:
    print('  body runs')

try:
    with Timer():
        raise ValueError('boom')
except ValueError as exc:
    print('caught outside:', exc)

  acquiring
  body runs
  releasing; exception was None
  acquiring
  releasing; exception was ValueError
caught outside: boom

The __exit__ return value is a genuine trap: returning a truthy value swallows the exception. Since a bare return gives None, the default is correct, and you should only return True deliberately — that is precisely how contextlib.suppress is implemented.

class Suppress:
    def __init__(self, *types):
        self.types = types
    def __enter__(self):
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        return exc_type is not None and issubclass(exc_type, self.types)

with Suppress(ZeroDivisionError):
    1 / 0
print('still running')

still running

Section 4 shows contextlib.contextmanager, which lets you write the same thing as a generator with one yield — usually the better choice for one-off cases. The class form is preferable when the manager holds real state, is reusable, or is also an async context manager.

2.10 Truthiness

if x: consults, in order: __bool__, then __len__, then defaults to True. Only that last fallback surprises people — an object with neither method is always truthy, which is why a custom class that "looks empty" still enters the if.

class Bag:
    def __init__(self, items):
        self.items = list(items)
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.items)

class Plain:
    pass

print(bool(Bag([])), bool(Bag([1])))
print(bool(Plain()))

False True
True

Define __bool__ when emptiness and falsiness differ — a database row of all zeros exists and should be truthy even though it is "empty" in some other sense. Note also that __len__ returning 0 makes the object falsy for free, so containers rarely need __bool__ at all.

2.11 Copying and Serialisation Hooks

Copying is a protocol too, and knowing it prevents a very common class of bug: a "copy" that shares mutable internals with the original.

import copy

class Team:
    def __init__(self, name, members):
        self.name, self.members = name, members

t = Team('red', ['ann', 'bo'])
shallow = copy.copy(t)
deep = copy.deepcopy(t)
shallow.members.append('cy')       # shared list!
print(t.members)
print(deep.members)

['ann', 'bo', 'cy']
['ann', 'bo']

copy.copy creates a new object whose attributes point at the same sub-objects; copy.deepcopy recursively copies them, tracking already-seen objects so that cycles do not loop forever. Customise with __copy__ and __deepcopy__ when the default is wrong — an object holding an open socket or a thread lock cannot be meaningfully deep-copied and should say so.

The same hooks drive pickle, Python's built-in object serialisation. __getstate__ returns what to save and __setstate__ restores it, which is how you exclude an unpicklable attribute:

import pickle

class Connection:
    def __init__(self, dsn):
        self.dsn = dsn
        self.socket = object()             # stands in for a real, unpicklable socket
    def __getstate__(self):
        state = self.__dict__.copy()
        del state['socket']                # never serialise the live handle
        return state
    def __setstate__(self, state):
        self.__dict__.update(state)
        self.socket = None                 # reconnect lazily

c = Connection('postgres://localhost/app')
restored = pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(c))
print(restored.dsn, restored.socket)

postgres://localhost/app None

A security warning that belongs next to every mention of pickle: unpickling executes arbitrary code by design, because the format includes instructions to call constructors. pickle.loads on untrusted bytes is remote code execution. Use JSON for anything crossing a trust boundary. Section 13 returns to this with the alternatives.

2.12 The Map

Keep this as a reference; you will implement perhaps a dozen of these in a career, but recognising them all makes unfamiliar code readable.

Group Methods
Construction & lifecycle __new__, __init__, __del__, __init_subclass__, __set_name__
Representation __repr__, __str__, __format__, __bytes__
Comparison & hashing __eq__, __ne__, __lt__, __le__, __gt__, __ge__, __hash__
Attributes __getattr__, __getattribute__, __setattr__, __delattr__, __dir__
Descriptors __get__, __set__, __delete__
Containers __len__, __length_hint__, __getitem__, __setitem__, __delitem__, __contains__, __missing__
Iteration __iter__, __next__, __reversed__, __aiter__, __anext__
Callables __call__
Numeric __add__, __sub__, __mul__, __matmul__, __truediv__, __floordiv__, __mod__, __divmod__, __pow__, __lshift__, __rshift__, __and__, __xor__, __or__ (+ r and i variants)
Unary & conversion __neg__, __pos__, __abs__, __invert__, __complex__, __int__, __float__, __index__, __round__, __trunc__
Context managers __enter__, __exit__, __aenter__, __aexit__
Truthiness __bool__
Copy & pickle __copy__, __deepcopy__, __getstate__, __setstate__, __reduce__
Classes & typing __class_getitem__, __instancecheck__, __subclasshook__

Exercises

Exercise 2.1 — A correct value object. Write a Temperature class storing degrees Celsius that: prints as 20.0°C for users and Temperature(20.0) for developers; compares and sorts by value; is usable as a dict key; and supports +/- with another Temperature and * with a number on either side.

Solution 
from functools import total_ordering

@total_ordering
class Temperature:
    __slots__ = ('celsius',)

    def __init__(self, celsius):
        self.celsius = float(celsius)

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Temperature({self.celsius})'

    def __str__(self):
        return f'{self.celsius:.1f}\N{DEGREE SIGN}C'

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Temperature):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.celsius == other.celsius

    def __lt__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Temperature):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.celsius < other.celsius

    def __hash__(self):
        return hash(self.celsius)

    def __add__(self, other):
        if isinstance(other, Temperature):
            return Temperature(self.celsius + other.celsius)
        return NotImplemented

    def __sub__(self, other):
        if isinstance(other, Temperature):
            return Temperature(self.celsius - other.celsius)
        return NotImplemented

    def __mul__(self, k):
        if isinstance(k, (int, float)):
            return Temperature(self.celsius * k)
        return NotImplemented

    __rmul__ = __mul__

a, b = Temperature(20), Temperature(20)
print(str(a), repr(a))
print(a == b, len({a, b}), sorted([Temperature(30), a, Temperature(-5)]))
print(a + Temperature(5), 2 * a, a * 2)
try:
    a + 5
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

20.0°C Temperature(20.0)
True 1 [Temperature(-5.0), Temperature(20.0), Temperature(30.0)]
25.0°C 40.0°C 40.0°C
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'Temperature' and 'int'

Note that the third line shows 25.0°C, not Temperature(25.0): print() calls str() on each argument, so __str__ wins there, while the sorted(...) list on the line above is a container and therefore shows __repr__.

The points that matter: __hash__ hashes exactly the field __eq__ compares; __slots__ plus float storage makes the object effectively immutable, which is what makes hashing it safe; NotImplemented produces the interpreter's own good error message; and __rmul__ = __mul__ is valid because multiplication by a scalar commutes.

Exercise 2.2 — Why is the copy shared? This cache is supposed to hand out independent snapshots. Explain the bug and give two different fixes.

import copy

class Snapshot:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data

original = Snapshot({'users': ['ann']})
clone = copy.copy(original)
clone.data['users'].append('bo')
print(original.data)
Solution

copy.copy is a shallow copy: it makes a new Snapshot whose data attribute points at the very same dictionary — which in turn holds the very same list. Mutating anything nested is visible through both objects, so the original prints {'users': ['ann', 'bo']}.

Fix one — ask for a deep copy at the call site:

import copy

class Snapshot:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data

original = Snapshot({'users': ['ann']})
clone = copy.deepcopy(original)
clone.data['users'].append('bo')
print(original.data, clone.data)

{'users': ['ann']} {'users': ['ann', 'bo']}

Fix two — make the class copy correctly by default, so callers cannot get it wrong:

import copy

class Snapshot:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
    def __copy__(self):
        return Snapshot(copy.deepcopy(self.data))

original = Snapshot({'users': ['ann']})
clone = copy.copy(original)
clone.data['users'].append('bo')
print(original.data, clone.data)

{'users': ['ann']} {'users': ['ann', 'bo']}

The second is better when independence is part of the type's meaning: it puts the guarantee in one place instead of trusting every caller to remember. The general lesson is that "copy" is ambiguous in any language with references, and Python makes you choose which one you mean.

Exercise 2.3 — A context manager that suppresses selectively. Write ignore_missing, a context manager that swallows FileNotFoundError but lets every other exception through, and prove both behaviours.

Solution 
class ignore_missing:
    def __enter__(self):
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        return exc_type is not None and issubclass(exc_type, FileNotFoundError)

with ignore_missing():
    open('/no/such/file')
print('suppressed, still running')

try:
    with ignore_missing():
        raise PermissionError('denied')
except PermissionError as exc:
    print('propagated:', exc)

suppressed, still running
propagated: denied

The whole behaviour lives in __exit__'s return value: truthy suppresses, falsy propagates. The exc_type is not None guard matters because __exit__ also runs on the success path with all three arguments set to None, and issubclass(None, ...) would raise TypeError there — turning a clean exit into a crash.

The standard library already has this as contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError), which you should prefer in real code; writing it once is how you learn what it is doing.

Exercise 2.4 — Reflected operators. Predict what each line prints, and explain the third one in terms of the three-stage lookup.

class Metres:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
    def __repr__(self):
        return f'{self.n}m'
    def __add__(self, other):
        print('  __add__ tried')
        if isinstance(other, Metres):
            return Metres(self.n + other.n)
        return NotImplemented
    def __radd__(self, other):
        print('  __radd__ tried')
        if isinstance(other, (int, float)):
            return Metres(self.n + other)
        return NotImplemented

print(Metres(3) + Metres(4))
print(5 + Metres(3))
print(Metres(3) + 5)
Solution 
  __add__ tried
7m
  __radd__ tried
8m
  __add__ tried
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'Metres' and 'int'

Line 1: both operands are Metres, so __add__ handles it directly and __radd__ is never consulted.

Line 2: int.__add__(5, Metres(3)) returns NotImplemented because int has never heard of Metres, so Python tries the reflected method on the right operand — Metres.__radd__(Metres(3), 5) — which accepts.

Line 3 is the one worth getting right, because the natural guess is wrong. Metres.__add__(Metres(3), 5) runs and declines. Python then tries the reflected method on the right operand, which is int.__radd__ — and that declines too. It does not fall back to the left operand's own __radd__. Reflected methods belong to the other operand by definition, so Metres.__radd__ never gets a turn and the operation raises. Notice the trace: only one __add__ tried line appears and no second __radd__ tried line.

So 5 + Metres(3) works while Metres(3) + 5 does not — an asymmetry that looks like a bug to callers. The fix is to accept the type where it is actually reachable, in __add__:

class Metres:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
    def __repr__(self):
        return f'{self.n}m'
    def __add__(self, other):
        if isinstance(other, Metres):
            return Metres(self.n + other.n)
        if isinstance(other, (int, float)):
            return Metres(self.n + other)
        return NotImplemented
    __radd__ = __add__          # addition commutes, so one implementation serves both

print(Metres(3) + 5, 5 + Metres(3), Metres(3) + Metres(4))

8m 8m 7m

The design lesson has two halves. Decline by returning NotImplemented rather than raising, so the other operand still gets its turn — and remember that "the other operand" is the only one that gets a reflected call, so every type you intend to support must be handled in the forward method too.

SECTION 3

Classes in Depth

Section 1 explained how attributes are found and section 2 explained the protocols objects implement. This section is about the machinery that sits between them: the tools Python gives you for controlling what a class is when it is created, and what its attributes do when they are touched.

Most of this material has a reputation for being advanced. Very little of it is difficult; it is just rarely explained in order.

3.1 A Class Body Is Just Code

The most useful thing to know about classes is that class is a statement that executes. The body runs top to bottom in a fresh namespace, and whatever names that namespace ends up holding become the class attributes.

print('before')

class Demo:
    print('  class body running')
    x = 1
    y = x + 1                     # ordinary code: x is in scope here
    for i in range(2):
        pass

print('after')
print(Demo.x, Demo.y, Demo.i)

before
  class body running
after
1 2 1

Note that the loop variable i leaked into the class namespace — because there is no magic, only a namespace being populated by ordinary execution. This is also why a class body cannot see names from an enclosing class, and why comprehensions inside a class body famously cannot see the class's other attributes: the comprehension gets its own scope.

Once the body finishes, Python calls the metaclass — type by default — with the class name, its bases, and that namespace. §3.9 returns to this.

3.2 Methods Are Functions Until You Look Them Up

A def inside a class body creates a plain function. It becomes a method only when accessed through an instance, and that transformation is done by the descriptor protocol (§3.4).

class Greeter:
    def hello(self):
        return f'hello from {self!r}'

    @classmethod
    def make(cls):
        return f'classmethod on {cls.__name__}'

    @staticmethod
    def util(x):
        return f'staticmethod got {x}'

g = Greeter()
print(type(Greeter.hello).__name__)      # a plain function
print(type(g.hello).__name__)            # bound to the instance
print(g.hello.__self__ is g)
print(Greeter.make(), Greeter.util(1))

function
method
True
classmethod on Greeter staticmethod got 1

The three kinds and when each is right:

  • Instance method — needs the instance. The default.
  • @classmethod — needs the class, not the instance. The canonical use is an alternative constructor, and it is correct under subclassing because cls is whatever class it was called on.
  • @staticmethod — needs neither. A function that belongs in the class's namespace for organisation.
class Duration:
    def __init__(self, seconds):
        self.seconds = seconds
    def __repr__(self):
        return f'{type(self).__name__}({self.seconds})'

    @classmethod
    def from_minutes(cls, minutes):
        return cls(minutes * 60)          # cls, not Duration

class PreciseDuration(Duration):
    pass

print(Duration.from_minutes(2))
print(PreciseDuration.from_minutes(2))    # returns the SUBCLASS

Duration(120)
PreciseDuration(120)

Hard-coding Duration(...) there would return the wrong class for every subclass — a bug that only appears once someone subclasses you.

3.3 property: Attributes That Run Code

A property turns attribute access into method calls without changing the interface. This is why Python has no culture of writing get_x()/set_x() up front: you can start with a plain attribute and add validation later without breaking a single caller.

class Celsius:
    def __init__(self, degrees):
        self.degrees = degrees            # goes through the setter

    @property
    def degrees(self):
        return self._degrees

    @degrees.setter
    def degrees(self, value):
        if value < -273.15:
            raise ValueError('below absolute zero')
        self._degrees = float(value)

    @property
    def fahrenheit(self):                 # computed, read-only
        return self._degrees * 9 / 5 + 32

c = Celsius(100)
print(c.degrees, c.fahrenheit)
c.degrees = 0
print(c.degrees, c.fahrenheit)
try:
    c.degrees = -300
except ValueError as exc:
    print('ValueError:', exc)
try:
    c.fahrenheit = 100
except AttributeError as exc:
    print('AttributeError:', exc)

100.0 212.0
0.0 32.0
ValueError: below absolute zero
AttributeError: property 'fahrenheit' of 'Celsius' object has no setter

Note that __init__ assigns to self.degrees, which runs the setter — so validation applies at construction too, with no duplicated code. A read-only property is simply one with no setter, and Python produces a clear error for you.

3.4 Descriptors

A descriptor is any object defining __get__, __set__ or __delete__, placed as a class attribute. It is the mechanism underneath methods, property, classmethod, staticmethod and __slots__ — learning it once explains all of them at the same time.

Recall the lookup order from §1.6: data descriptors (defining __set__ or __delete__) beat the instance dictionary; non-data descriptors (only __get__) lose to it. That single asymmetry is why a method can be shadowed by an instance attribute but a property cannot.

class Positive:
    """A data descriptor: validates on every assignment."""
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        self.name = '_' + name            # told its own attribute name
    def __get__(self, obj, objtype=None):
        if obj is None:
            return self                   # accessed on the class
        return getattr(obj, self.name)
    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        if value <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f'{self.name[1:]} must be positive, got {value}')
        setattr(obj, self.name, value)

class Rectangle:
    width = Positive()
    height = Positive()
    def __init__(self, width, height):
        self.width, self.height = width, height
    def area(self):
        return self.width * self.height

r = Rectangle(3, 4)
print(r.area())
try:
    r.width = -1
except ValueError as exc:
    print('ValueError:', exc)
print(type(Rectangle.width).__name__)     # obj is None -> returns the descriptor

12
ValueError: width must be positive, got -1
Positive

Two validated attributes, one validator, written once. A property would need the logic duplicated per attribute; that is exactly when to reach for a descriptor instead.

__set_name__ (Python 3.6) is what makes this ergonomic: at class creation Python calls it on every descriptor in the body, telling it the attribute name it was assigned to. Without it you would have to write width = Positive('width') and keep the string in sync by hand.

Now the payoff — the standard tools are all descriptors:

class C:
    def method(self): ...
    @property
    def prop(self): return 1
    @staticmethod
    def stat(): ...
    __slots__ = ()

print('function is a non-data descriptor:',
      hasattr(C.method, '__get__'), hasattr(C.method, '__set__'))
print('property is a data descriptor:',
      hasattr(C.prop, '__get__'), hasattr(C.prop, '__set__'))

function is a non-data descriptor: True False
property is a data descriptor: True True

That is the whole explanation for a behaviour that otherwise looks arbitrary: obj.method = something works and shadows the method, because a function is a non-data descriptor and loses to the instance dict. obj.prop = something raises, because property is a data descriptor and wins.

3.5 Multiple Inheritance and the MRO

When a class has several bases, Python needs a deterministic order in which to search them. That order is the MRO (method resolution order), computed by the C3 linearisation, and it guarantees that a class always precedes its own bases and that the order of bases is preserved.

class A:
    def who(self): return 'A'
class B(A):
    def who(self): return 'B -> ' + super().who()
class C(A):
    def who(self): return 'C -> ' + super().who()
class D(B, C):
    def who(self): return 'D -> ' + super().who()

print([c.__name__ for c in D.__mro__])
print(D().who())

['D', 'B', 'C', 'A', 'object']
D -> B -> C -> A

Look carefully at that second line, because it is the point of the whole mechanism. B.who calls super().who() — and super() inside B resolved to C, not to A, even though B inherits from A and knows nothing about C.

super() does not mean "my parent". It means "the next class in the MRO of the actual instance". That is what makes cooperative multiple inheritance work: the diamond's shared base A runs exactly once, not twice.

The practical rules for cooperative classes:

  • Every class in the hierarchy must call super(), or the chain breaks at the first one that does not.
  • Signatures must be compatible along the chain, which is why mixins conventionally accept and forward **kwargs.
  • If C3 cannot produce a consistent order, the class definition itself raises TypeError — the inconsistency is caught at definition time, not at call time.
class Base:
    def __init__(self, **kw):
        self.log = ['Base']
class Loud(Base):
    def __init__(self, **kw):
        super().__init__(**kw)
        self.log.append('Loud')
class Timed(Base):
    def __init__(self, **kw):
        super().__init__(**kw)
        self.log.append('Timed')
class Service(Loud, Timed):
    def __init__(self, **kw):
        super().__init__(**kw)
        self.log.append('Service')

print(Service().log)

try:
    class Broken(Base, Loud): ...
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', str(exc)[:60])

['Base', 'Timed', 'Loud', 'Service']
TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order (MRO) for

The log reads bottom-up because each __init__ appends after delegating — every class runs, once, in reverse MRO order.

3.6 Abstract Base Classes

An abstract base class declares an interface that subclasses must implement, and refuses to instantiate anything incomplete. Where a Protocol (§6.6) checks shape structurally at type-check time, an ABC enforces inheritance at runtime.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Storage(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def save(self, key: str, value: bytes) -> None: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def load(self, key: str) -> bytes: ...

    def save_text(self, key: str, text: str) -> None:   # concrete: shared logic
        self.save(key, text.encode())

class MemoryStorage(Storage):
    def __init__(self):
        self._data = {}
    def save(self, key, value):
        self._data[key] = value
    def load(self, key):
        return self._data[key]

class Incomplete(Storage):
    def save(self, key, value): ...          # forgot load()

s = MemoryStorage()
s.save_text('greeting', 'hello')
print(s.load('greeting'))
try:
    Incomplete()
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

b'hello'
TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Incomplete without an implementation for abstract method 'load'

The failure happens at instantiation, not at definition — which is what allows an abstract subclass to add some methods and leave others for its own children.

collections.abc ships the interfaces the language itself uses — Iterable, Sequence, Mapping, Hashable — and inheriting from them gives you working mixin methods for free:

from collections.abc import Sequence

class Deck(Sequence):
    def __init__(self, cards):
        self._cards = list(cards)
    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self._cards[i]
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self._cards)

d = Deck(['A', 'K', 'Q'])
print('Q' in d, d.index('K'), list(reversed(d)), d.count('A'))

True 1 ['Q', 'K', 'A'] 1

Two methods written; __contains__, index, count, __iter__ and __reversed__ all supplied by the ABC. ABC or Protocol? Use an ABC when you own the hierarchy and want shared implementation plus runtime enforcement; use a Protocol when you are typing objects you do not own, or want structural matching with no inheritance.

3.7 __init_subclass__: The Hook Before Metaclasses

Most reasons people reach for a metaclass are better served by __init_subclass__, which runs on the parent whenever a subclass is defined.

class Plugin:
    registry = {}

    def __init_subclass__(cls, /, name=None, **kwargs):
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        key = name or cls.__name__.lower()
        Plugin.registry[key] = cls

class JsonPlugin(Plugin): ...
class CsvPlugin(Plugin, name='csv-reader'): ...

print(sorted(Plugin.registry))
print(Plugin.registry['csv-reader'] is CsvPlugin)

['csv-reader', 'jsonplugin']
True

Self-registering subclasses, validation of subclass definitions, and injected defaults — all without a metaclass, and with none of a metaclass's inheritance conflicts. Note it can accept keyword arguments passed in the class header, which is how CsvPlugin supplied its own name.

The companion hook is __set_name__ (§3.4), for the descriptor side. Between them they cover the large majority of class-creation customisation.

3.8 Metaclasses

A metaclass is the class of a class. type is the default, and calling type(name, bases, namespace) is exactly what the class statement does.

def make_greet(self):
    return 'hi'

Dynamic = type('Dynamic', (), {'x': 1, 'greet': make_greet})
print(Dynamic.__name__, Dynamic().x, Dynamic().greet())
print(type(Dynamic), type(int), type(type))

Dynamic 1 hi
<class 'type'> <class 'type'> <class 'type'>

A custom metaclass subclasses type and overrides __new__ or __init__ to intervene at class creation:

class Validated(type):
    def __new__(mcls, name, bases, ns, **kw):
        if bases and not ns.get('__doc__'):
            raise TypeError(f'{name} must have a docstring')
        ns['created_by'] = 'Validated'
        return super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, ns, **kw)

class Model(metaclass=Validated):
    """Base."""

class Good(Model):
    """Documented."""

print(Good.created_by)
try:
    class Bad(Model): pass
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

Validated
TypeError: Bad must have a docstring

When to actually use one. Almost never. The honest list is: when you must change the namespace before the class object exists, when you need to control isinstance/issubclass via __instancecheck__, or when you are building a framework whose users write declarative class bodies — which is why ORMs and abc itself use them.

The real cost is composability: a class can have only one metaclass, and combining two classes with different metaclasses is a TypeError your users cannot fix. __init_subclass__ has no such problem. The standard guidance stands:

If you are wondering whether you need a metaclass, you do not. People who genuinely need them know they do.

3.9 Dataclasses in Depth

@dataclass generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from annotated class attributes. It is the right default for any class that is mostly data.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True, kw_only=True)
class Point:
    x: float
    y: float
    label: str = 'origin'
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)   # NOT tags: list = []

p = Point(x=1, y=2)
print(p)
print(p == Point(x=1, y=2))
try:
    p.x = 5
except AttributeError as exc:
    print('AttributeError:', exc)
try:
    hash(p)                                       # a mutable field is still in there
except TypeError as exc:
    print('TypeError:', exc)

Point(x=1, y=2, label='origin', tags=[])
True
AttributeError: cannot assign to field 'x'
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'

That last line is the trap worth learning. frozen=True generates a __hash__ over all the fields, which is precisely §2.4's contract — but it cannot make a list field hashable, and the failure appears when someone first calls hash(), not at class definition. A frozen dataclass is hashable only if every field is. Use a tuple instead of a list, or exclude the field:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Point:
    x: float
    y: float
    tags: tuple[str, ...] = ()                    # immutable -> hashable

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Other:
    x: float
    notes: list[str] = field(default_factory=list, compare=False, hash=False)

print(hash(Point(1, 2)) == hash(Point(1, 2)))
print(len({Point(1, 2), Point(1, 2)}))
print(hash(Other(1)) == hash(Other(1)))

True
1
True

The options that matter:

  • frozen=True makes instances immutable and hashable — provided every field is itself hashable, as above. This is the default you want for value objects.
  • slots=True (3.10) adds __slots__, giving §1.7's memory saving with none of the boilerplate.
  • kw_only=True (3.10) forces keyword arguments, so adding a field later cannot silently reorder positional calls.
  • field(default_factory=...) is mandatory for mutable defaults — a bare tags: list = [] raises ValueError at class creation, because the dataclass machinery recognises §1.2's bug and refuses.
from dataclasses import dataclass

try:
    @dataclass
    class Bad:
        items: list = []
except ValueError as exc:
    print('ValueError:', exc)

ValueError: mutable default <class 'list'> for field items is not allowed: use default_factory

Other useful pieces: field(compare=False) excludes a field from __eq__, field(repr=False) hides a secret from logs, __post_init__ runs after generated initialisation for derived values, and dataclasses.replace() produces a modified copy of a frozen instance.

For comparison: NamedTuple is immutable, indexable and tuple-compatible — good for lightweight records; TypedDict (§6.7) types a plain dict with no class at runtime; pydantic (§13) validates at runtime. Dataclasses sit in the middle and are the usual answer.

3.10 Enums

An Enum gives a fixed set of named constants that are singletons, comparable by identity, and self-documenting in tracebacks and logs.

from enum import Enum, StrEnum, IntFlag, auto

class Status(Enum):
    PENDING = 'pending'
    ACTIVE = 'active'

class Colour(StrEnum):                 # 3.11: is a real str
    RED = 'red'
    GREEN = 'green'

class Perm(IntFlag):
    READ = auto()
    WRITE = auto()
    EXEC = auto()

print(Status.ACTIVE, Status.ACTIVE.value, Status('active') is Status.ACTIVE)
print(Colour.RED == 'red', f'{Colour.RED} works in strings')
rw = Perm.READ | Perm.WRITE
print(repr(rw), Perm.WRITE in rw, Perm.EXEC in rw)
print(rw, int(rw))                     # str() is int's, since 3.11
print([s.name for s in Status])

Status.ACTIVE active True
True red works in strings
<Perm.READ|WRITE: 3> True False
3 3
['PENDING', 'ACTIVE']

Note the difference between the two flag lines. repr() shows the readable <Perm.READ|WRITE: 3>, but str() gives 3 — since Python 3.11 IntEnum, IntFlag and StrEnum inherit their __str__ from int/str rather than from Enum, specifically so they interpolate into strings and format as the underlying value. It is what you want for serialisation and a surprise in log messages, so reach for repr() or .name when you are logging a flag.

StrEnum and IntEnum are the interoperability escape hatches — members really are str/int, so they serialise to JSON and compare with raw values, at the cost of being implicitly usable where a plain string was expected. IntFlag gives you combinable bit flags with readable reprs. Use @enum.unique to forbid aliases, and auto() when the values themselves carry no meaning.

Exercises

Exercise 3.1 — Why does this validation not run? The author expected assigning to temp to be validated. Explain why it is not, and fix it.

class Reading:
    def __init__(self, temp):
        self.temp = temp

    def temp(self):
        if self.temp < -273.15:
            raise ValueError('too cold')
        return self.temp
Solution

Two separate problems, and the first hides the second.

temp is defined as a plain method, which is a non-data descriptor. Per §1.6 and §3.4, non-data descriptors lose to the instance dictionary — so self.temp = temp in __init__ writes straight into self.__dict__, shadowing the method entirely. Nothing is ever validated, and Reading(5).temp returns 5 rather than a bound method.

Even if it were reached, the method is infinitely recursive: self.temp inside temp would call itself.

A property is a data descriptor, so it wins over the instance dict and cannot be shadowed. The stored value needs a different name to avoid the recursion:

class Reading:
    def __init__(self, temp):
        self.temp = temp                  # goes through the setter

    @property
    def temp(self):
        return self._temp

    @temp.setter
    def temp(self, value):
        if value < -273.15:
            raise ValueError('too cold')
        self._temp = value

r = Reading(20)
print(r.temp)
try:
    r.temp = -300
except ValueError as exc:
    print('ValueError:', exc)
try:
    Reading(-300)
except ValueError as exc:
    print('rejected at construction too:', exc)

20
ValueError: too cold
rejected at construction too: too cold

The general lesson is the data/non-data asymmetry: if you want an attribute that cannot be bypassed by assignment, it must define __set__. That is exactly the difference between a method and a property.

Exercise 3.2 — Predict the MRO. Give D.__mro__ and the output of D().go(), then explain why B's super() reaches what it does.

class A:
    def go(self): return ['A']
class B(A):
    def go(self): return ['B'] + super().go()
class C(A):
    def go(self): return ['C'] + super().go()
class D(C, B):
    def go(self): return ['D'] + super().go()
Solution 
class A:
    def go(self): return ['A']
class B(A):
    def go(self): return ['B'] + super().go()
class C(A):
    def go(self): return ['C'] + super().go()
class D(C, B):
    def go(self): return ['D'] + super().go()

print([c.__name__ for c in D.__mro__])
print(D().go())

['D', 'C', 'B', 'A', 'object']
['D', 'C', 'B', 'A']

Note the bases are (C, B) here, the reverse of §3.5's example, and the MRO reverses with them: C3 preserves the order in which bases are declared.

The instructive part is C.go calling super().go() and reaching B — a class C does not inherit from and has no knowledge of. super() is not "my parent"; it is "the next class after me in type(self).__mro__". Since self is a D, that MRO is D → C → B → A, so C's super() is B.

This is the entire reason A.go runs once rather than twice. If each class had hard-coded A.go(self) instead of super(), the diamond would call A twice — the classic multiple-inheritance bug that C3 and cooperative super() exist to prevent.

Because behaviour depends on the MRO of the runtime instance, a mixin cannot know statically who follows it. That is why cooperative classes forward **kwargs and always call super().

Exercise 3.3 — Replace repetition with a descriptor. This class validates three fields with near-identical code. Rewrite it so the validation is written once, and the error message still names the right field.

class Product:
    def __init__(self, price, weight, quantity):
        if price <= 0: raise ValueError('price must be positive')
        self._price = price
        if weight <= 0: raise ValueError('weight must be positive')
        self._weight = weight
        if quantity <= 0: raise ValueError('quantity must be positive')
        self._quantity = quantity
Solution

A data descriptor holds the rule once; __set_name__ supplies the field name so the message stays specific.

class Positive:
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        self._name = name
        self._store = '_' + name

    def __get__(self, obj, objtype=None):
        if obj is None:
            return self
        return getattr(obj, self._store)

    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        if value <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f'{self._name} must be positive')
        setattr(obj, self._store, value)

class Product:
    price = Positive()
    weight = Positive()
    quantity = Positive()

    def __init__(self, price, weight, quantity):
        self.price, self.weight, self.quantity = price, weight, quantity

p = Product(10, 2, 5)
print(p.price, p.weight, p.quantity)
for field, args in [('price', (0, 1, 1)), ('weight', (1, -1, 1)), ('quantity', (1, 1, 0))]:
    try:
        Product(*args)
    except ValueError as exc:
        print('ValueError:', exc)

10 2 5
ValueError: price must be positive
ValueError: weight must be positive
ValueError: quantity must be positive

Three fields, one validator, and validation still applies on later assignment (p.price = -1 raises) because __set__ runs on every write — something the original __init__-only checks did not do.

Two details that matter. __get__ must handle obj is None and return the descriptor itself, or Product.price raises instead of being introspectable. And the value is stored under a different name (_price) than the descriptor occupies (price); storing it under the same name would make __set__ call itself forever.

When to prefer what: one validated attribute is a property; three or more sharing a rule is a descriptor; a whole class of validated fields declared from types is pydantic (§13), which is descriptors all the way down.

Exercise 3.4 — Registry without a metaclass. A plugin system uses a metaclass to auto-register subclasses. Rewrite it without one, and explain what problem that removes.

class PluginMeta(type):
    registry = {}
    def __new__(mcls, name, bases, ns):
        cls = super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, ns)
        if bases:
            PluginMeta.registry[name.lower()] = cls
        return cls

class Plugin(metaclass=PluginMeta):
    pass
Solution

__init_subclass__ does the same job as a plain classmethod on the base:

class Plugin:
    registry = {}

    def __init_subclass__(cls, /, name=None, **kwargs):
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        Plugin.registry[name or cls.__name__.lower()] = cls

class JsonPlugin(Plugin): ...
class XmlPlugin(Plugin, name='xml'): ...

print(sorted(Plugin.registry))
print(Plugin.registry['xml'] is XmlPlugin)

['jsonplugin', 'xml']
True

The problem it removes is metaclass conflict. A class has exactly one metaclass, and that metaclass must be a subclass of the metaclasses of all its bases. So with the original design, a user who wants a plugin that is also an abc.ABC gets:

TypeError: metaclass conflict: the metaclass of a derived class must be a (non-strict) subclass of the metaclasses of all its bases

— because ABCMeta and PluginMeta are unrelated. The user cannot fix this without editing your library. With __init_subclass__ there is no metaclass at all, so class Thing(Plugin, ABC) simply works.

The rewrite also gains keyword arguments in the class header (name='xml') essentially for free, and is materially easier to read for anyone who has not memorised the type.__new__ signature. This is why §3.8's guidance is that the genuine remaining uses for metaclasses are narrow: controlling isinstance, or needing to alter the namespace before the class object exists.

SECTION 4

Functions, Closures and Decorators

Functions in Python are ordinary objects that happen to be callable. Once that clicks, decorators stop being syntax to memorise and become an obvious consequence: if a function is a value, you can write a function that takes one and returns another.

4.1 Functions Are Objects

A def statement creates an object and binds it to a name. That object carries attributes you can read, modify and use.

def greet(name: str, greeting: str = 'Hello') -> str:
    """Return a greeting."""
    return f'{greeting}, {name}!'

print(greet.__name__, '|', greet.__doc__)
print(greet.__defaults__, greet.__annotations__['return'])

alias = greet                       # just another name for the same object
