2. Use the right data structure. As above — usually a one-line change.

3. Hoist invariants out of loops.

import re, time

text = 'the year 2026 and the year 1999'
pattern = r'\d{4}'

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(20_000):
    re.findall(pattern, text)                # re-looks-up the compiled cache
uncompiled = time.perf_counter() - t0

compiled = re.compile(pattern)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(20_000):
    compiled.findall(text)                   # no lookup at all
precompiled = time.perf_counter() - t0

print('precompiling helped:', precompiled < uncompiled)

precompiling helped: True

4. Build strings with join, not += in a loop. Repeated concatenation is O(n²) because each + copies everything so far.

import time

n = 40_000
t0 = time.perf_counter()
s = ''
for i in range(n):
    s += 'x'
concat = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
s2 = ''.join('x' for _ in range(n))
joined = time.perf_counter() - t0

print('same result:', s == s2)
print('join was faster:', joined < concat)

same result: True
join was faster: True

5. Prefer built-ins and comprehensions. sum, min, sorted, any and list comprehensions run their loops in C rather than in the interpreter.

6. Use __slots__ or dataclass(slots=True) when instance count is in the millions (§1.7).

7. Use local variables in hot loops. Local lookups are an array index; global and attribute lookups are dictionary lookups. append = out.append before a tight loop is a real, if small, win — and a readability cost, so only where profiling justifies it.

10.7 When Python Itself Is the Limit

If the algorithm is right and it is still too slow, the remaining options leave pure Python behind.

  • NumPy — vectorised array operations in C, with the GIL released. For numerical work this is usually a 10–100× improvement and should be the first thing tried, not the last.
  • A C extension — the traditional route. You write C against the CPython API, or use ctypes/cffi to call an existing shared library without compiling anything yourself.
  • Cython — annotate Python with static types and compile it to a C extension. The gentlest path from working Python to fast native code.
  • PyO3 / Rust — increasingly the modern choice for new extensions; memory-safe, and what pydantic-core, ruff and uv are built with.
  • The JIT. CPython 3.13 added an experimental copy-and-patch JIT, and 3.14 ships it in the official Windows and macOS binaries. It is off by default and its gains are modest so far; it is a direction of travel rather than a lever to pull today.
  • PyPy — an alternative interpreter with a mature tracing JIT, often several times faster on long-running pure-Python workloads. The constraint is C extension compatibility.
import ctypes, ctypes.util

libm = ctypes.CDLL(ctypes.util.find_library('m'))
libm.sqrt.restype = ctypes.c_double            # you MUST declare the types
libm.sqrt.argtypes = [ctypes.c_double]
print(libm.sqrt(144.0))

12.0

That is C called from Python with no compiler involved. Note the explicit restype/argtypes: ctypes assumes int returns otherwise, and omitting them produces silently wrong numbers rather than an error.

Before reaching for any of this, confirm the problem is CPU-bound Python. If it is I/O, sections 8 and 9 are the answer; if it is a database, an index (or one fewer query) will beat any of this by an order of magnitude.

Exercises

Exercise 10.1 — Find and fix the bottleneck. This takes far longer than it should. Profile it mentally, name the complexity, and fix it.

def find_duplicates(records):
    duplicates = []
    for i, record in enumerate(records):
        if record in records[i + 1:]:
            if record not in duplicates:
                duplicates.append(record)
    return duplicates
Solution

Three separate O(n) operations nested inside an O(n) loop:

  1. records[i + 1:] builds a new list on every iteration — O(n) copying, n times, so O(n²) just in allocation.
  2. record in records[i + 1:] is an O(n) scan.
  3. record not in duplicates is another O(n) scan.

Overall O(n²) with a large constant. A Counter does it in one pass:

import collections, time

def find_duplicates_slow(records):
    duplicates = []
    for i, record in enumerate(records):
        if record in records[i + 1:]:
            if record not in duplicates:
                duplicates.append(record)
    return duplicates

def find_duplicates(records):
    counts = collections.Counter(records)
    return [item for item, n in counts.items() if n > 1]

data = [i % 800 for i in range(4000)]
t0 = time.perf_counter(); slow = find_duplicates_slow(data); slow_t = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter(); fast = find_duplicates(data); fast_t = time.perf_counter() - t0

print('same answer:', sorted(slow) == sorted(fast))
print('items found:', len(fast))
print('at least 10x faster:', slow_t > fast_t * 10)

same answer: True
items found: 800
at least 10x faster: True

Counter is O(n) and hashes each record once. Note the requirement it introduces: records must be hashable (§1.5). If they are dicts, key on a tuple of the fields that define identity, or use frozenset(d.items()).

The general pattern to recognise: a membership test inside a loop over the same data is nearly always O(n²) and nearly always fixable with a set or a Counter. Slicing inside a loop is the other tell — it is easy to miss because it looks like indexing.

Exercise 10.2 — Which measurement tool? For each symptom, say which tool you would reach for and what you would look at.

  1. A web request takes 3 seconds and you do not know why.
  2. A worker process grows from 200 MB to 4 GB over a day.
  3. You want to know whether dict.get(k, d) is faster than try/except KeyError.
  4. A production service is wedged right now and you cannot restart it.
Solution

1. Three-second request — cProfile, sorted by cumtime. Sort by cumulative time first to find the call path responsible, then by tottime to find the function actually burning CPU. If neither shows much CPU, the time is I/O — a database query or an HTTP call — and the profiler will show it as time inside a read/recv. In that case the answer is in section 9, not here. For a real service, prefer a sampling profiler or distributed tracing so you are measuring production rather than a synthetic run.

2. Growth to 4 GB — tracemalloc. Snapshot after warm-up, snapshot again later, compare_to(..., 'lineno') and read the top entries: they name the exact allocation site of memory still held. Common causes are an unbounded cache (§4.8 — functools.cache on a method), a module-level list that only ever grows, and reference cycles holding large objects (§1.9). gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_LEAK) helps with the last of these. objgraph is worth knowing for visualising what refers to what.

3. dict.get vs try/except — timeit. This is exactly what micro-benchmarks are for. Benchmark both branches, though: try/except is very cheap when the key is usually present and relatively expensive when it usually is not, so the answer depends on your hit rate. Then remember §10.2's second rule and check the function is hot enough for the difference to matter at all.

4. Wedged service — attach to it. py-spy dump --pid <PID> shows the current stack of every thread with no restart and near-zero overhead; py-spy top gives a live view. On Python 3.14, python -m pdb -p <PID> (PEP 768) attaches the standard debugger to a running process, and python -m asyncio ps <PID> shows the asyncio task tree (§9.11). Look for a thread blocked on a lock, a socket read with no timeout, or a deadlock between two locks acquired in different orders.

The pattern: CPU → cProfile or a sampler; memory → tracemalloc; micro-comparison → timeit; live process → attach, never restart. Restarting destroys the evidence.

SECTION 11

Imports, Environments and Packaging

Everything so far has been about code that runs. This section is about code that ships: how Python finds the modules you import, how environments keep one project's dependencies from breaking another's, and how a directory of .py files becomes something a colleague can pip install. These are the parts of Python most often learned by superstition — a sys.path.append that fixes an import for reasons nobody can explain, a requirements.txt that produces a different set of packages every time it is installed. All of it is mechanical, and once you have seen the mechanism the superstitions go away.

11.1 What import Actually Does

import json looks like a keyword doing something magical. It is not. Python's import system is four steps, all of them written in Python and all of them inspectable — importlib in the standard library is the import system, and the import statement is a call into it.

1. Check sys.modules — a plain dict of every module already imported. A hit ends the process immediately; this is why importing something twice is free.
2. Ask each finder in sys.meta_path for a spec. The last one, PathFinder, is the one that walks sys.path.
3. The spec's loader creates a module object, inserts it into sys.modules before executing it, then runs the file's code in that module's namespace.
4. Bind a name in the importing namespace. import json binds json; from json import loads binds loads.
import sys
import importlib.util

print('json loaded already?', 'json' in sys.modules)
import json
print('json loaded now?    ', 'json' in sys.modules)
print('the name and the cache entry are one object:', json is sys.modules['json'])

spec = importlib.util.find_spec('json')          # step 2, without doing step 3
print('name:  ', spec.name)
print('loader:', type(spec.loader).__name__)
print('origin:', '/'.join(spec.origin.split('/')[-2:]))
print('is a package (has search locations):', spec.submodule_search_locations is not None)

print('sys origin:', importlib.util.find_spec('sys').origin)
print('sys is compiled into the interpreter:', 'sys' in sys.builtin_module_names)
# meta_path holds classes as often as instances, so ask for the right name:
names = [f.__name__ if isinstance(f, type) else type(f).__name__ for f in sys.meta_path]
print('the last three finders:', names[-3:])

json loaded already? False
json loaded now?     True
the name and the cache entry are one object: True
name:   json
loader: SourceFileLoader
origin: json/__init__.py
is a package (has search locations): True
sys origin: built-in
sys is compiled into the interpreter: True
the last three finders: ['BuiltinImporter', 'FrozenImporter', 'PathFinder']

Three consequences worth holding on to.

Module-level code runs exactly once per process. A module body is not a definition, it is a script that happens to define things. If it opens a database connection or reads an environment variable, that happens at import time, in whatever order the imports resolve — which is why import-time side effects are a recurring source of bugs that only appear in one deployment.

sys.modules is writable. Deleting an entry forces a re-import; assigning a fake module is how unittest.mock.patch replaces a dependency (§12.6). importlib.reload(mod) re-executes the file in the existing module object, so old references survive — which is why reload is useful in a REPL and dangerous anywhere else.

Builtins have no file. sys reports origin: built-in: it was compiled into the interpreter, and BuiltinImporter claims it before PathFinder ever looks at the disk. That ordering is why you cannot shadow sys with a local sys.py, but can shadow json.

Which modules are compiled in is a property of the build, not of the language. On the Linux build this course was written on, math was built in too. In the macOS Homebrew build of 3.14 it is a separate extension module under lib-dynload, found by PathFinder like any other file — so there, a local math.py in the script's directory does shadow it. sys.builtin_module_names lists what is compiled into the interpreter in front of you, and it is the only reliable answer.

11.2 sys.path: Where Python Looks

PathFinder walks sys.path in order and takes the first match. The list is assembled at startup from four sources, and knowing which entry comes first explains most "why is it importing the wrong thing" incidents.

Position Entry Comes from
First the script's directory python app.py → the directory containing app.py
First the current directory ('') python -c ..., python -m mod, and the REPL
Then $PYTHONPATH entries the environment variable, split on :
Then the standard library the interpreter's own installation
Last site-packages added by the site module at startup

The first row is the trap. Name a file random.py, email.py, types.py or token.py and every import of that name in your project — including imports made by libraries you did not write — resolves to your file instead. The failure is rarely a clean ImportError; it is usually an AttributeError from deep inside a dependency.

python -c "import random; print(random.__file__)"   # confirm what you actually got
python -P app.py             # 3.11+: do NOT put the script's directory first
PYTHONSAFEPATH=1 python app.py                      # same thing, as an env var

Python 3.14 added a related diagnostic. When an import fails and the failing module lives in the directory you launched Python from, the error gains a hint: consider renaming /path/to/random.py if it has the same name as a library you intended to import. It is a genuinely useful nudge — but note the cost, because it costs a different message: that hint replaces the circular-import hint, so a circular import between two top-level modules in your working directory reports a filename clash instead of the cycle. Move the same two modules into a package and the message becomes "partially initialized module … most likely due to a circular import". Same bug, two different explanations.

Appending to sys.path at runtime works and is almost always the wrong fix. It hides the real problem — a project that is not installed — and it only works for code launched from one specific directory. The right fix is §11.9: an installable project, installed in editable mode.

11.3 Packages and __init__.py

A package is a directory Python imports as a module. shop/__init__.py makes shop a package; importing shop.models.order executes shop/__init__.py, then shop/models/__init__.py, then shop/models/order.py, in that order — importing a submodule always imports its ancestors first.

import sys, tempfile, pathlib, textwrap

root = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(root / "shop" / "models").mkdir(parents=True)

(root / "shop" / "__init__.py").write_text(textwrap.dedent("""
    print("shop/__init__.py runs")
    from .models.order import Order          # re-export, so callers say shop.Order
    __all__ = ["Order"]
"""))
(root / "shop" / "models" / "__init__.py").write_text('print("shop/models/__init__.py runs")\n')
(root / "shop" / "models" / "order.py").write_text(textwrap.dedent("""
    print("shop/models/order.py runs")
    class Order:
        def __init__(self, total): self.total = total
"""))

sys.path.insert(0, str(root))
import shop

print("---")
print("public name:", shop.Order(19.99).total)
print("everything imported:", sorted(n for n in sys.modules if n.startswith("shop")))
print("shop.__path__ has one directory:", len(shop.__path__) == 1)

shop/__init__.py runs
shop/models/__init__.py runs
shop/models/order.py runs
---
public name: 19.99
everything imported: ['shop', 'shop.models', 'shop.models.order']
shop.__path__ has one directory: True

What belongs in __init__.py. Re-exports that define the package's public surface, __all__, and nothing expensive. What does not belong: database connections, config loading, logging configuration (§7.8), and long import chains. Every one of those runs before the caller has done anything, and a package whose __init__.py imports its entire subtree makes import shop cost as much as importing all of shop. §11.7 shows how to defer that.

__all__ does two things and neither is access control. It sets what from shop import * binds, and it tells type checkers and linters which names are deliberate re-exports rather than accidental leakage. Nothing stops anyone importing a name you left out.

11.4 Namespace Packages

A directory with no __init__.py can still be imported — as a namespace package (PEP 420, Python 3.3+). Its distinguishing property is that it can be assembled from several directories on sys.path at once.

import sys, tempfile, pathlib

root = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
for portion, sub in (("dist-a", "alpha"), ("dist-b", "beta")):
    d = root / portion / "acme" / sub          # note: no acme/__init__.py anywhere
    d.mkdir(parents=True)
    (d / "__init__.py").write_text(f'NAME = "{sub}"\n')
    sys.path.insert(0, str(root / portion))

import acme.alpha, acme.beta
print("both halves import:", acme.alpha.NAME, acme.beta.NAME)
print("acme.__file__:", acme.__file__)
print("__path__ type:", type(acme.__path__).__name__)
print("portions found:", len(list(acme.__path__)))

both halves import: alpha beta
acme.__file__: None
__path__ type: _NamespacePath
portions found: 2

acme has no file of its own, and its __path__ is a live _NamespacePath that re-scans sys.path when it changes. That is the whole feature: two separately distributed packages, acme-alpha and acme-beta, can both install into acme/ and coexist. Large organisations use this for a shared top-level namespace across many repositories.

Use it deliberately, or not at all. The common encounter with namespace packages is accidental: you forget an __init__.py, the directory becomes a namespace package, and imports mostly work — until the day a test runner collects two directories with the same name and silently merges them, or a build backend excludes your code from the wheel because it was not recognised as a package. If a directory is one package, give it an __init__.py. Empty is fine.

11.5 Relative Imports and python -m

Inside a package, from .models import Order is a relative import: one dot means "this package", two means "the parent". Relative imports are resolved from __package__, not from the filesystem, which is why they behave differently depending on how you started Python.

from . import config              # sibling module in the same package
from .models.order import Order   # deeper in the same package
from ..shared import retry        # up one level, then down

Run python shop/cli.py and __package__ is empty, __name__ is "__main__", and every relative import fails with ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package. Run python -m shop.cli and Python imports the shop package first, sets __package__ = "shop", and the same imports resolve.

The rule: run modules inside packages with -m. It also fixes sys.path[0] — -m puts the current directory there rather than the script's directory, so the package is importable at all. -m is why python -m pytest, python -m venv and python -m http.server are written that way.

The if __name__ == "__main__": guard is the same mechanism seen from the other side. A module's __name__ is its import name normally, and "__main__" when it is the program's entry point. The guard means "only when run directly", and it is not optional decoration: multiprocessing with the spawn start method (§8.6) re-imports your __main__ module in the child, and without the guard the child re-runs your program.

A package can also be executed: python -m shop runs shop/__main__.py. That file, plus a console script (§11.13), is how a package gets a command-line interface.

11.6 Circular Imports

Two modules that import each other are a cycle. Whether it fails depends on precisely when each name is needed.

import sys, tempfile, pathlib, textwrap

root = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(root / "app").mkdir()
(root / "app" / "__init__.py").write_text("")
(root / "app" / "orders.py").write_text(textwrap.dedent("""
    from app.invoices import make_invoice
    class Order:
        def bill(self): return make_invoice(self)
"""))
(root / "app" / "invoices.py").write_text(textwrap.dedent("""
    from app.orders import Order
    def make_invoice(order): return f"invoice for {type(order).__name__}"
"""))
sys.path.insert(0, str(root))

try:
    import app.orders
except ImportError as exc:
    print(type(exc).__name__ + ":", str(exc).split(" (/")[0])   # trim the file path
    print("failing module:", exc.name)

ImportError: cannot import name 'Order' from partially initialized module 'app.orders' (most likely due to a circular import)
failing module: app.orders

Read the sequence and the message stops being mysterious. app.orders starts executing and is placed in sys.modules immediately — as an empty module. Its first line imports app.invoices, which imports app.orders, gets the cache hit, and asks for Order, which the class statement has not reached yet. "Partially initialized" is literal.

Three fixes, in order of preference.

  1. Break the cycle. A cycle is usually a design signal: the two modules share a concept that belongs in a third. Move Order to app/models.py and have both import from there.
  2. Import the module, not the name. import app.orders inside invoices.py, then use app.orders.Order at call time. Module objects exist from the first line; the attribute is only looked up when the function runs, by which point both modules are complete. Note this only works if the use is inside a function — at module level it fails identically.
  3. Import inside the function. A deferred import is a legitimate tool, not a hack. It costs one sys.modules dict lookup per call.

For imports needed only by annotations, there is a fourth answer that costs nothing at runtime. typing.TYPE_CHECKING is a constant that is False at runtime and True to every type checker, so an import inside if TYPE_CHECKING: is read by mypy and never executed:

from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

if TYPE_CHECKING:                       # never runs; mypy reads it anyway
    from app.invoices import Invoice

def latest(order: "Order") -> "Invoice | None":
    ...

On Python 3.14 the annotations themselves are already lazy (§6.2), so the names need no quotes there; the quotes above are what you write for 3.13 and earlier, where from __future__ import annotations gives the same behaviour. Either way, a cycle that exists purely because two modules annotate each other's types is not a real cycle.

11.7 Lazy Imports and Import Hooks

A library with a large surface faces a conflict: from toolkit import Frame should work, but importing toolkit should not drag in NumPy for someone who only wanted the CSV parser. PEP 562 (3.7+) resolves it with a module-level __getattr__, called only when normal attribute lookup on the module fails.

import sys, tempfile, pathlib, textwrap

root = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(root / "toolkit").mkdir()
(root / "toolkit" / "__init__.py").write_text(textwrap.dedent('''
    __all__ = ["parse_csv", "Frame"]

    def __getattr__(name):                     # PEP 562: module-level __getattr__
        if name == "Frame":
            from .heavy import Frame
            return Frame
        raise AttributeError(f"module {__name__!r} has no attribute {name!r}")

    def __dir__():                             # keep tab-completion honest
        return sorted(__all__)

    def parse_csv(text):
        return [line.split(",") for line in text.splitlines()]
'''))
(root / "toolkit" / "heavy.py").write_text(
    'print("   heavy.py is executing")\nclass Frame:\n    pass\n')
sys.path.insert(0, str(root))

import toolkit
print("after import, heavy loaded?", "toolkit.heavy" in sys.modules)
print("cheap call:", toolkit.parse_csv("a,b\nc,d"))
print("now touching toolkit.Frame:")
Frame = toolkit.Frame
print("heavy loaded now?", "toolkit.heavy" in sys.modules)
print("dir(toolkit):", dir(toolkit))
try:
    toolkit.nope
except AttributeError as exc:
    print("AttributeError:", exc)

after import, heavy loaded? False
cheap call: [['a', 'b'], ['c', 'd']]
now touching toolkit.Frame:
   heavy.py is executing
heavy loaded now? True
dir(toolkit): ['Frame', 'parse_csv']
AttributeError: module 'toolkit' has no attribute 'nope'

Two details make this production-grade rather than a trick. The fallback raise AttributeError is required — without it, every failed lookup returns None and hasattr lies. And __dir__ (also PEP 562) is what keeps dir() and REPL completion showing the lazy names, which __getattr__ alone cannot do because there is nothing to enumerate.

Below that sits the import system's extension point for the truly unusual case: sys.meta_path. Inserting a finder there lets you import from a database, a zip file, an encrypted archive, or nothing at all. This is how zipimport works, how import-time instrumentation works, and how tools that need to see every import — coverage measurement, lazy-loading frameworks — hook in. You will read code that does this more often than you will write it, but knowing the list is ordered and writable is the difference between "magic" and "a list of objects with a find_spec method".

python -X importtime app.py prints the cumulative and self time of every import, which is the correct way to find out whether any of this is worth doing. Startup time is nearly always import time.

11.8 Virtual Environments

Two projects need different versions of the same library. Without isolation, one of them is broken. A virtual environment is the isolation, and it is far simpler than its reputation: a directory with its own site-packages, a pyvenv.cfg file, and symlinks to an existing interpreter.

python3 -m venv .venv          # create
source .venv/bin/activate      # Linux/macOS
.venv\Scripts\activate         # Windows
deactivate                     # leave

$ cat .venv/pyvenv.cfg
home = /usr/bin
include-system-site-packages = false
version = 3.14.4
executable = /usr/bin/python3.14
command = /usr/bin/python3 -m venv /home/ada/project/.venv

That file is the virtual environment. When the interpreter at .venv/bin/python starts, it finds pyvenv.cfg next to itself, sets sys.prefix to the venv and sys.base_prefix to home, and builds sys.path with the venv's site-packages instead of the system one. The standard library still comes from the base installation — a venv copies almost nothing.

$ .venv/bin/python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix); print(sys.base_prefix)"
/home/ada/project/.venv
/usr

sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix is the reliable test for "am I in a virtual environment", and it works without activation.

Activation is only convenience. All activate does is prepend .venv/bin to $PATH (and set VIRTUAL_ENV), so that python and pip resolve to the venv's copies. .venv/bin/python -m pip install requests does exactly the same thing with no activation at all — which is what you want in a Dockerfile, a systemd unit or a cron job, where there is no shell to activate anything in.

Four rules that prevent the usual mess:

  • One venv per project, in the project, named .venv, and git-ignored. Every tool looks for that name.
  • Never sudo pip install. It writes into the interpreter your operating system depends on. Modern Python refuses anyway: the externally-managed-environment error (PEP 668) exists precisely to stop this, and --break-system-packages is named as a warning, not a suggestion.
  • Do not commit the venv. It contains absolute paths and platform-specific binaries. Commit the lockfile (§11.11) instead.
  • python -m pip, not pip. It guarantees the pip you run belongs to the interpreter you mean. A bare pip on $PATH may belong to something else entirely.

For throwaway command-line tools, pipx (or uv tool install) installs each into its own private venv and puts only the entry point on $PATH — the right way to install ruff, httpie or black globally without them sharing dependencies.

11.9 pyproject.toml

pyproject.toml (PEP 518/621) is the single declarative description of a Python project: what it is, what it needs, how to build it, and how its tools are configured. It replaced setup.py, setup.cfg, requirements.txt and a scattering of tool-specific dotfiles.

[build-system]                       # who builds this, and what they need
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]                            # PEP 621 metadata — backend-independent
name = "textwrangler"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Tidy up messy text files."
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
license = "MIT"
authors = [{ name = "Ada Lovelace", email = "ada@example.com" }]
dependencies = ["click>=8.1"]

[project.optional-dependencies]      # extras: pip install textwrangler[fast]
fast = ["orjson>=3.9"]

[dependency-groups]                  # PEP 735: for developers, never installed by users
dev = ["pytest>=8", "mypy>=1.11", "ruff>=0.6"]

[project.scripts]                    # becomes a `wrangle` command on PATH
wrangle = "textwrangler.cli:main"

[project.urls]
Homepage = "https://github.com/ada/textwrangler"

[tool.ruff]                          # tool config lives here too
line-length = 100

Three tables, three jobs. [build-system] is read first, by the frontend (pip, uv, build), which installs those requirements into an isolated environment and hands control to the named backend — hatchling, setuptools, flit_core, pdm-backend, uv_build, or maturin for Rust extensions. [project] is standardised metadata that every backend understands identically. [tool.*] is a namespace each tool owns; ruff, mypy, pytest and coverage all read their configuration from here.

Use the src layout.

textwrangler/
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
├── src/
│   └── textwrangler/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       └── cli.py
└── tests/
    └── test_cli.py

Putting the package under src/ means the project directory is not on sys.path, so your tests cannot accidentally import the source tree instead of the installed package. That sounds pedantic until a package ships with a missing module that every local test passed against, because the tests were importing the working copy rather than the wheel. The src layout makes that failure impossible.

Install it into the active venv in editable mode, which is how you work on it:

python -m pip install -e .              # editable: code changes take effect immediately
python -m pip install -e ".[fast]"      # with an extra
python -m pip install --group dev       # PEP 735 group (pip 25.1+)

Editable installs work by putting a path hook in site-packages that points at src/. Nothing is copied, so there is no stale-copy problem — but note that newly added entry points and metadata changes still need a re-install, because those are recorded in the .dist-info directory at install time.

11.10 Building: sdist and Wheel

Two distribution formats, and the difference matters.

An sdist (textwrangler-0.1.0.tar.gz) is the source: your package, pyproject.toml, README, and a PKG-INFO. Installing one requires running the build backend on the target machine.

A wheel (textwrangler-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl) is the built artefact: a zip file whose contents are laid straight into site-packages. No build step, no arbitrary code executed at install time. Wheels are why installing is fast.

python -m pip install build
python -m build              # writes both into dist/

$ python -m build
* Creating isolated environment: venv+pip...
* Installing packages in isolated environment:
  - hatchling
* Getting build dependencies for sdist...
* Building sdist...
* Building wheel from sdist
Successfully built textwrangler-0.1.0.tar.gz and textwrangler-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl

Note the third line: build makes the wheel from the sdist, not from your working directory. That catches the most common packaging bug — a file that works locally because it is on disk and is missing from the distribution.

A wheel is a zip; open it.

$ unzip -l dist/textwrangler-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
textwrangler/__init__.py
textwrangler/cli.py
textwrangler/filters.py
textwrangler-0.1.0.dist-info/METADATA
textwrangler-0.1.0.dist-info/WHEEL
textwrangler-0.1.0.dist-info/entry_points.txt
textwrangler-0.1.0.dist-info/RECORD

Note what is not there: no src/ (the backend strips it), no tests/, no pyproject.toml. METADATA holds the [project] table rendered into the standard format, RECORD lists every file with a SHA-256 hash and a size, and WHEEL describes the format itself.

The filename is structured — {name}-{version}-{python tag}-{abi tag}-{platform tag}.whl:

Filename Means
textwrangler-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl pure Python, any Python 3, any platform — one wheel serves everyone
numpy-2.3.5-cp314-cp314-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl compiled for CPython 3.14 on 64-bit Linux
numpy-2.3.5-cp314-cp314t-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl the t suffix is the free-threaded build (§8.8)

pip picks the most specific wheel matching your interpreter and platform, and falls back to the sdist only if there is none — which is when you discover you need a C compiler. When a compiled dependency has no wheel for your platform, that is the reason, and the fix is a different platform, an older version, or a manylinux wheel from the maintainers.

11.11 Dependencies, Constraints and Lockfiles

A dependency specifier is a name plus an optional constraint (PEP 508).

Specifier Means
click any version — almost never what you want
click>=8.1 8.1 or newer, no upper bound
click>=8.1,<9 the usual shape: allow fixes, exclude the next major
click~=8.1.2 compatible release: >=8.1.2,<8.2.0
click==8.1.7 exactly this — correct for an application's lockfile, wrong in a library
orjson; python_version < "3.13" an environment marker: only install where the condition holds

Libraries and applications need opposite policies. A library should declare the widest range it actually supports, because a hard pin in a library becomes an unresolvable conflict for anyone who depends on two libraries with different pins. An application should pin everything, transitively, so that today's deploy and next month's deploy install the same bytes.

That second requirement is what a lockfile is for. pyproject.toml states intent (click>=8.1); the lockfile records the resolution (click==8.1.7, plus every transitive dependency, plus a hash of each artefact). You commit both, and the difference between them is exactly the difference between "what we need" and "what we tested".

[[package]]
name = "httpx"
version = "0.28.1"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
dependencies = [
    { name = "anyio" },
    { name = "certifi" },
    { name = "httpcore" },
    { name = "idna" },
]
sdist = { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/.../httpx-0.28.1.tar.gz", hash = "sha256:6..." }
wheels = [
    { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/.../httpx-0.28.1-py3-none-any.whl", hash = "sha256:d..." },
]

Those hashes are the security property, not a detail. An install from a lockfile verifies each downloaded file against a hash you committed, so a compromised index or a re-uploaded artefact fails the install rather than shipping.

A hand-written requirements.txt is not a lockfile. It usually lists direct dependencies only, with loose constraints and no hashes, so two installs a month apart can differ in dozens of transitive packages. The tools that do produce real lockfiles are uv (uv.lock), pip-tools (pip-compile → a fully pinned, hashed requirements.txt), poetry (poetry.lock) and pdm (pdm.lock). Pick one; the failure mode is not choosing.

11.12 uv

uv is a package and project manager written in Rust that replaces pip, venv, pip-tools, pipx and pyenv behind one command, and is fast enough to change how you work — resolution and installation that took a minute take under a second, so uv sync in a hook stops being an annoyance.

uv init --lib reportgen        # create a project: pyproject.toml, src/, .python-version
uv add "httpx>=0.27"           # resolve, install, update pyproject.toml AND uv.lock
uv add --dev pytest ruff mypy  # into the dev dependency group
uv remove httpx
uv sync                        # make .venv match uv.lock exactly
uv sync --frozen               # ...and fail if the lock is out of date (use this in CI)
uv lock --upgrade-package httpx
uv run pytest                  # run a command in the project env, syncing first
uv python install 3.14         # it manages interpreters too
uv tool install ruff           # pipx equivalent: isolated env, entry point on PATH
uvx ruff check .               # run a tool without installing it at all

$ uv add "httpx>=0.27"
Resolved 9 packages in 412ms
Installed 8 packages in 96ms
 + anyio==4.14.2
 + certifi==2026.7.22
 + h11==0.16.0
 + httpcore==1.0.9
 + httpx==0.28.1
 + idna==3.19
 + typing-extensions==4.16.0

The mental model differs from pip's in one important way: you do not activate a venv and install into it. You describe the project, and uv makes .venv match the lockfile whenever you run something. uv run syncs first, so the environment cannot silently drift from the file you committed. uv pip install exists as a compatibility layer for the old workflow, and it is a transition aid rather than the intended path.

None of this is required knowledge for reading Python, and all of it is required for working in a team that has adopted it — which, since 2024, is a rapidly growing share of them. The concepts are the same ones in §11.11; only the speed and the ergonomics changed.

11.13 Entry Points

An entry point is a name in your package's metadata that other code can look up without importing your package first. Two kinds matter.

Console scripts turn a function into a command. wrangle = "textwrangler.cli:main" under [project.scripts] makes the installer generate an executable named wrangle in the environment's bin/ that imports textwrangler.cli and calls main(). The function takes no arguments and its return value becomes the exit code — return 1 or call sys.exit(1) to signal failure (§13.3).

Plugin groups are the general form, and they are how a library lets strangers extend it. pytest finds its plugins this way, as do flake8, sphinx and pygments. Declare a group in pyproject.toml; anyone who installs a package that advertises that group is discovered automatically.

import sys, tempfile, pathlib
from importlib.metadata import entry_points, version, distribution

# What an installer writes into site-packages. Building it by hand shows there
# is no magic here: entry points are a text file inside a .dist-info directory.
tmp = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
dist = tmp / "textwrangler-0.1.0.dist-info"
dist.mkdir()
(dist / "METADATA").write_text(
    "Metadata-Version: 2.5\nName: textwrangler\nVersion: 0.1.0\n"
    "Requires-Dist: click>=8.1\n")
(dist / "entry_points.txt").write_text(
    "[console_scripts]\nwrangle = textwrangler.cli:main\n\n"
    "[textwrangler.filters]\nupper = textwrangler.filters:upper\n")
sys.path.insert(0, str(tmp))

print("version: ", version("textwrangler"))
print("requires:", distribution("textwrangler").requires)

for ep in entry_points(group="textwrangler.filters"):
    print(f"  plugin {ep.name!r} -> module={ep.module} attr={ep.attr}")
    # ep.load() would import the module and return the object.

print("console script:", [e.value for e in entry_points(group="console_scripts", name="wrangle")])

version:  0.1.0
requires: ['click>=8.1']
  plugin 'upper' -> module=textwrangler.filters attr=upper
console script: ['textwrangler.cli:main']

The host application's side is a loop over entry_points(group=...) calling ep.load(). Note the property that makes this worth the ceremony: discovery costs no imports. Reading metadata is a file read, so an application can list twenty available plugins and import only the one that is used. importlib.metadata is also where version() comes from, which is the correct way for a package to report its own version — read it from the installed metadata rather than duplicating a string in __init__.py that will drift from pyproject.toml.

11.14 Publishing

python -m build                                   # dist/*.whl and dist/*.tar.gz
python -m pip install twine
twine check dist/*                                # does the README render on PyPI?
twine upload --repository testpypi dist/*         # rehearse on TestPyPI first
twine upload dist/*                               # the real thing

Four things to get right before the first upload.

Claim the name early; PyPI names are first-come and cannot be transferred casually. Check availability before you settle on one.

Use Trusted Publishing rather than an API token. Configure your PyPI project to trust a specific GitHub Actions workflow in a specific repository, and the workflow exchanges an OIDC identity for a short-lived token at publish time. There is no long-lived secret to leak, rotate, or accidentally commit. If you must use a token, scope it to the single project, never to the whole account.

A version can never be replaced. PyPI refuses a re-upload of an existing version, deliberately, so that a hash pinned in someone's lockfile always means the same bytes. A bad release is fixed by publishing the next version. yank (PEP 592) is the intermediate tool: a yanked version stays installable for anyone who pinned it exactly, and is ignored by resolvers choosing a new version — the right response to a release with a serious bug.

Version deliberately. Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) is the default expectation: patch for fixes, minor for backwards-compatible additions, major for anything that breaks callers. Calendar versioning (2026.8.1) suits applications and things that track the outside world. Either is fine; picking neither is not, because your version number is a promise other people's constraint specifiers rely on. Use 0.x while you are still willing to break things, and deprecate with a DeprecationWarning for at least one minor release before removing anything.

Finally, the release checklist that catches nearly everything: build, twine check, install the built wheel into a fresh venv, import it, run its console script, and only then upload. Testing the wheel rather than the working tree is the whole point — it is the only way to find out what you forgot to include.

Exercises

Exercise 11.1 — Diagnose four import failures. For each, name the mechanism and give the fix.

  1. A script that works from the project root fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'shop' when run from anywhere else.
  2. from .models import Order raises ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package.
  3. A colleague's machine imports a json module that is missing loads.
  4. Tests pass locally, and the published wheel is missing shop/utils.py entirely.
Solution

1. sys.path[0] is the script's directory, not the project root. It works from the root because the current directory happened to contain shop/. The fix is not sys.path.append — it is to make the project installable (pyproject.toml with the src layout) and pip install -e . into the venv. Then shop is importable from any directory, in tests, and in production, for the same reason.

2. Run it with -m. A file executed as a script has __name__ == "__main__" and no __package__, so there is no "current package" for the dot to be relative to. python -m shop.cli imports shop first and sets __package__, and the relative import resolves. The other half of the fix, if this is a CLI, is to declare a console script (§11.13) so users never type either form.

3. A json.py in the current directory shadows the standard library. PathFinder walks sys.path in order, and the script's directory is first. Confirm with python -c "import json; print(json.__file__)", then rename the file — and delete the __pycache__/json.*.pyc next to it, which will otherwise still be found. On 3.14 the error message may say so itself: consider renaming …. Note that the same trick does not work for math, which is a builtin and is claimed by BuiltinImporter before sys.path is consulted at all.

4. The tests were importing the source tree, not the package. A flat layout puts the project root on sys.path, so import shop finds the working copy and never touches what the backend actually packaged. Move to src/, and make the release check "install the wheel into a fresh venv and import it" rather than "run the tests".

The unifying idea: three of the four are the same bug. sys.path contains a directory you did not intend, and something was found there instead of where you meant.

Exercise 11.2 — Write the pyproject.toml. A library called csvkit-lite exposing a csvlite command, requiring Python 3.11+, depending on click 8.1 or newer but not 9, with an optional excel extra pulling in openpyxl, and dev tooling of pytest, ruff and mypy. Use hatchling and the src layout.

Solution 
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "csvkit-lite"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A small CSV toolkit."
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
license = "MIT"
authors = [{ name = "Your Name", email = "you@example.com" }]
dependencies = ["click>=8.1,<9"]

[project.optional-dependencies]
excel = ["openpyxl>=3.1"]

[dependency-groups]
dev = ["pytest>=8", "ruff>=0.6", "mypy>=1.11"]

[project.scripts]
csvlite = "csvkit_lite.cli:main"

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["src/csvkit_lite"]

Four points that are easy to get wrong.

The distribution name and the import name differ. csvkit-lite on PyPI, csvkit_lite in import. That is normal (pillow/PIL, beautifulsoup4/bs4), and the hyphen is not legal in an import name. Names are normalised for comparison — csvkit-lite, csvkit_lite and CSVKit.Lite are the same project to a resolver.

<9 belongs in a library; ==8.1.7 does not. Two libraries that both pin exactly and disagree cannot be installed together at all.

The dev tools are in [dependency-groups], not [project.optional-dependencies]. An extra is part of your published metadata — anyone can pip install csvkit-lite[dev] and it is downloaded from PyPI. A PEP 735 group is local to the source checkout and is never published, which is where test and lint tooling belongs.

The [tool.hatch...] table is needed because the distribution name does not match the directory. Hatchling infers src/csvkit_lite/ from a name of csvkit-lite in the simple cases; state it explicitly and the build cannot guess wrong.

Exercise 11.3 — Make this package cheap to import. analytics/__init__.py takes 1.4 seconds to import because of the first three lines. Rewrite it so that importing the package is fast, from analytics import load_frame still works, and analytics.CONFIG is still available.

# analytics/__init__.py
import pandas as pd
from .frames import load_frame
from .plotting import plot_series

CONFIG = _read_config_file()          # reads ~/.analytics.toml at import time
Solution 
# analytics/__init__.py
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

__all__ = ["load_frame", "plot_series", "CONFIG"]

if TYPE_CHECKING:                     # type checkers see the real names...
    from .frames import load_frame
    from .plotting import plot_series

_config = None

def __getattr__(name):                # ...and at runtime nothing is imported until used
    global _config
    if name == "load_frame":
        from .frames import load_frame
        return load_frame
    if name == "plot_series":
        from .plotting import plot_series
        return plot_series
    if name == "CONFIG":
        if _config is None:
            _config = _read_config_file()
        return _config
    raise AttributeError(f"module {__name__!r} has no attribute {name!r}")

def __dir__():
    return sorted(__all__)

import pandas disappears entirely — it was never used in __init__.py, only in frames.py, and it will be imported when frames is. That one line is usually most of the 1.4 seconds.

CONFIG becomes lazy and cached. Reading a file at import time is the more serious defect of the two: it makes import analytics fail on a machine with no config file, it makes the value impossible to override in a test, and it happens even for callers that never look at it. Deferring it to first access fixes all three.

TYPE_CHECKING keeps the tooling working. A module-level __getattr__ is invisible to a type checker, so without that block from analytics import load_frame becomes an error in mypy and loses autocompletion. The block costs nothing at runtime (§11.6).

Measure before and after with python -X importtime -c "import analytics". And note the trade-off honestly: import errors in frames.py now surface at first use rather than at import, which is worse for a small package. Lazy imports are for packages with heavy or optional dependencies, not for every __init__.py.

Exercise 11.4 — Application or library? For each decision, say which policy applies and why.

  1. Pin requests==2.32.3 in pyproject.toml.
  2. Commit uv.lock.
  3. Publish a 0.x version for a year.
  4. Add numpy to dependencies because one optional feature uses it.
Solution

1. Application: correct — but in the lockfile, not pyproject.toml. Even for an application the two files have different jobs: pyproject.toml says what you support, the lock says what you tested. Pinning in both means every upgrade is two edits. Library: wrong, and actively harmful — a hard pin propagates to every consumer and conflicts with any other library that pinned differently. Declare requests>=2.32,<3.

2. Application: yes, always. It is the artefact that makes deploys reproducible and the hashes that make them verifiable. Library: no — nothing installs your lockfile, since a consumer resolves your constraints against everything else in their tree. Committing it for local development is fine, but treat it as a dev convenience and test against the oldest versions you claim to support as well as the newest, or your lower bounds are fiction.

3. Both: fine, and honest. 0.x communicates "the interface may change". The failure is staying there indefinitely while thousands depend on you — at that point the version number is lying, and a 1.0 costs nothing.

4. Wrong for both. A dependency needed by one optional feature belongs in [project.optional-dependencies] as an extra, imported lazily (§11.7) and guarded with a clear error if missing. Putting it in dependencies forces a ~60 MB download on everyone who installs your package for the other features.

The one-line version: a library states the widest range it truly supports and pins nothing; an application pins everything and commits the lock. A project that is both — a library with a CLI — follows the library rule for its metadata and keeps a lockfile for its own CI.

SECTION 12

Testing and Code Quality

A test suite is not a box to tick. It is the thing that lets you change code you no longer remember writing, and the difference between a codebase that gets better over time and one that ossifies. This section covers the tools professional Python projects actually run — pytest, coverage, Hypothesis, ruff, mypy, pre-commit — and, more importantly, how to use them so that a green suite means something.

12.1 What a Test Is For

A test answers one question: if I change this, will I find out that I broke it? Everything else — coverage percentages, test counts, framework choice — is instrumental to that.

Three properties separate a suite people trust from one they learn to ignore.

Deterministic. The same code gives the same result every run. A test that fails one run in twenty trains everyone to re-run it, and then to ignore it.
Independent. Any test can run alone, and in any order. Shared mutable state between tests is the most common cause of "it passes locally".
About behaviour, not implementation. A test that asserts how a function works breaks every time you refactor, which is exactly when you needed it to hold still.

The structure of a good test is Arrange, Act, Assert, in that order and visibly separated: set up the world, do the one thing under test, check one outcome. If a test has three "Act" steps it is really three tests, and when it fails you will not know which one broke.

Name tests for the behaviour they pin down. test_line_total_applies_discount tells you what broke from the failure line alone; test_1 sends you reading code.

12.2 pytest and Assertion Rewriting

unittest ships with Python and follows the JUnit tradition — a TestCase subclass, self.assertEqual, setUp and tearDown. It works, and you will read it in older codebases. Everything new uses pytest, because a test is a plain function and an assertion is a plain assert.

# tests/test_pricing.py
import pytest
from cart.pricing import line_total

def test_line_total_applies_discount():
    assert line_total(10.0, 3, discount=0.1) == 27.0

def test_rejects_negative_quantity():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="negative"):
        line_total(10.0, -1)

def test_broken_on_purpose():
    order = {"id": 7, "items": ["apple", "pear"], "total": 27.0}
    assert order == {"id": 7, "items": ["apple", "plum"], "total": 27.5}

A bare assert normally throws away everything about why it failed. pytest gets that back by rewriting the bytecode of your test modules at import time, so a failing comparison can report both sides:

$ pytest
============================= test session starts ==============================
platform linux -- Python 3.14.4, pytest-9.1.1, pluggy-1.6.0
rootdir: /home/ada/cart
configfile: pyproject.toml
testpaths: tests
collected 3 items

tests/test_pricing.py ..F                                                [100%]

=================================== FAILURES ===================================
____________________________ test_broken_on_purpose ____________________________

    def test_broken_on_purpose():
        order = {"id": 7, "items": ["apple", "pear"], "total": 27.0}
>       assert order == {"id": 7, "items": ["apple", "plum"], "total": 27.5}
E       AssertionError: assert {'id': 7, 'it...'total': 27.0} == {'id': 7, 'it...'total': 27.5}
E
E         Omitting 1 identical items, use -vv to show
E         Differing items:
E         {'items': ['apple', 'pear']} != {'items': ['apple', 'plum']}
E         {'total': 27.0} != {'total': 27.5}
E         Use -v to get more diff

tests/test_pricing.py:13: AssertionError
=========================== short test summary info ============================
FAILED tests/test_pricing.py::test_broken_on_purpose - AssertionError: assert...
========================= 1 failed, 2 passed in 0.11s ==========================

Read what it did: it identified the two differing keys out of three and hid the identical one. That diffing is per-type — sets report missing and extra members, strings report the first differing position, and long sequences report the index. This is why assert a == b in pytest is more informative than self.assertEqual(a, b), not less.

The flags that carry the day-to-day work:

pytest                       # everything
pytest tests/test_pricing.py::test_rejects_negative_quantity   # one test
pytest -x                    # stop at the first failure
pytest --lf                  # re-run only last-failed
pytest --ff                  # failures first, then the rest
pytest -k "discount and not slow"     # select by name substring expression
pytest -m integration        # select by marker
pytest -q                    # quiet;  -v verbose;  -vv full diffs
pytest -s                    # do not capture stdout (print() becomes visible)
pytest --pdb                 # drop into the debugger at the failure (§7.9)
pytest -p no:randomly -n auto         # disable a plugin / run on all cores (pytest-xdist)

--lf and -x together are the tight loop: fix, re-run only what was broken, repeat.

12.3 Discovery, Layout and Configuration

pytest finds tests by convention: files matching test_*.py or *_test.py, functions starting with test_, and classes named Test* (without an __init__). Nothing is registered; renaming a file out of that pattern silently removes its tests from the suite, which is worth remembering when a suite mysteriously shrinks.

cart/
├── pyproject.toml
├── src/cart/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   └── pricing.py
└── tests/
    ├── conftest.py            # fixtures and hooks, discovered automatically
    ├── test_pricing.py
    └── integration/
        └── test_checkout.py

Configuration belongs in pyproject.toml with everything else:

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
addopts = "-ra --strict-markers --strict-config"
markers = [
    "slow: takes more than a second",
    "integration: needs a real database",
]
filterwarnings = ["error", "ignore::DeprecationWarning:third_party.*"]

Four settings that earn their place. -ra prints a summary of everything that was not a plain pass, so skips and xfails stop being invisible. --strict-markers turns a typo'd marker into an error rather than a silently-never-selected test — without it, @pytest.mark.integraton is accepted and its test runs in every suite. --strict-config does the same for unknown config keys. And filterwarnings = ["error"] promotes warnings to failures, which is how you find out about a deprecation while there is still time to act rather than on the day it becomes an exception.

The src layout matters here for the reason given in §11.9: tests import cart the way users do, from the installed package, so a module missing from the wheel fails in CI rather than shipping. Install the project into the venv (pip install -e .) and never add sys.path manipulation to conftest.py.

12.4 Fixtures

A fixture is a function whose return value is injected into any test that names it as a parameter. It replaces setUp/tearDown with something composable: fixtures can request other fixtures, and each is created once per whatever scope you give it.

# tests/conftest.py — fixtures here are available to every test below this directory
import pytest

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def database():
    print("\n  [session] start database")
    yield {"users": []}                    # everything before yield is setup
    print("\n  [session] stop database")   # everything after is teardown

@pytest.fixture
def user(database):                        # fixtures compose: this one requests another
    record = {"name": "ada"}
    database["users"].append(record)
    yield record
    database["users"].remove(record)       # runs even if the test fails

# tests/test_fx.py
def test_one(user, database):
    assert database["users"] == [user]

def test_two(user, database):
    assert len(database["users"]) == 1     # the previous test cleaned up after itself

--setup-show prints the lifecycle, which is the fastest way to understand what is being created and when:

$ pytest --setup-show -q
SETUP    S database
        SETUP    F user (fixtures used: database)
        tests/test_fx.py::test_one (fixtures used: database, user) .
        TEARDOWN F user
        SETUP    F user (fixtures used: database)
        tests/test_fx.py::test_two (fixtures used: database, user) .
        TEARDOWN F user
TEARDOWN S database
2 passed in 0.05s

S is session scope, F is function scope. The expensive thing is built once; the per-test state is built and destroyed around each test. That combination — share what is slow, isolate what is mutable — is the entire art of fixtures.

Scope Created once per Use for
function (default) each test anything mutable
class test class rare
module test file a moderately expensive read-only resource
package test package same, one level up
session whole run database container, browser, loaded model

The teardown must be in the fixture, not the test. The code after yield runs whether the test passed, failed, or raised — that is the guarantee. A try/finally in a test does not cover a failure in setup.

Two more capabilities worth knowing. request.addfinalizer(fn) registers extra cleanup at runtime, and @pytest.fixture(params=[...]) makes a parametrised fixture: every test using it runs once per parameter, which is how you run a whole suite against three database backends without touching the tests.

conftest.py is the mechanism for sharing. It is discovered automatically by directory — a fixture in tests/conftest.py is visible to every test under tests/, and one in tests/integration/conftest.py only to that subtree. Never import it; never put tests in it.

12.5 Parametrisation

One test body, many cases. The point is not brevity — it is that each case is reported separately, so a failure names the input that broke.

import pytest
from cart.pricing import line_total

@pytest.mark.parametrize("price, quantity, discount, expected", [
    (10.0, 1, 0.0, 10.0),
    (10.0, 3, 0.1, 27.0),
    (0.0, 5, 0.5, 0.0),
    pytest.param(19.99, 2, 0.25, 29.98, id="float-rounding"),
])
def test_line_total(price, quantity, discount, expected):
    assert line_total(price, quantity, discount) == expected

$ pytest -v
tests/test_param.py::test_line_total[10.0-1-0.0-10.0] PASSED             [ 25%]
tests/test_param.py::test_line_total[10.0-3-0.1-27.0] PASSED             [ 50%]
tests/test_param.py::test_line_total[0.0-5-0.5-0.0] PASSED               [ 75%]
tests/test_param.py::test_line_total[float-rounding] PASSED              [100%]

============================== 4 passed in 0.03s ===============================

Four independent test cases, each with an id you can pass straight back to pytest to re-run it alone. pytest.param(..., id=...) replaces the auto-generated id, and takes marks= too — pytest.param(..., marks=pytest.mark.xfail) marks a single case as expected-to-fail without splitting the test up.

That last case is a real result and worth pausing on: 19.99 * 2 * 0.75 displays as 29.985, and round(...) of it is 29.98, not 29.99. The stored float is fractionally below 29.985, so there is nothing to round up. This is not a pytest quirk; it is §1 arithmetic showing up where it will actually cost you money. For currency, keep integer cents or decimal.Decimal — and note that a parametrised table is exactly how you would pin that decision down.

Stacking two parametrize decorators produces the cross-product, which is occasionally what you want and more often an accident:

@pytest.mark.parametrize("currency", ["eur", "usd"])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("quantity", [1, 2, 3])
def test_matrix(currency, quantity):        # 6 cases
    ...

Keep the case table data, not logic. If a parametrised test needs an if on which case it is in, it is two tests wearing one coat.

12.6 Test Doubles: monkeypatch, Mock, and Where to Patch

Real code talks to networks, clocks and filesystems. A test double replaces one of those with something predictable. Python offers three tools, in increasing order of power and of the damage they can do.

monkeypatch is the pytest fixture for setting an attribute, dict item or environment variable for the duration of one test, and putting it back afterwards. It is the right default because the undo is automatic.

def test_uses_configured_region(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv("AWS_REGION", "eu-west-1")
    monkeypatch.setattr("cart.pricing.TAX_RATE", 0.2)
    monkeypatch.delenv("AWS_PROFILE", raising=False)
    monkeypatch.chdir(tmp_path)
    ...

unittest.mock is the standard library's recording stand-in. A MagicMock accepts any call and any attribute, records everything, and can be interrogated afterwards.

from unittest.mock import MagicMock, create_autospec

gateway = MagicMock(name="gateway")
gateway.charge.return_value = {"id": "ch_1", "status": "succeeded"}

result = gateway.charge(amount=1999, currency="eur")
print("returned:", result)
print("called once:", gateway.charge.call_count == 1)
gateway.charge.assert_called_once_with(amount=1999, currency="eur")
print("call args:", gateway.charge.call_args)

# side_effect: a sequence of results, or an exception to raise
gateway.refund.side_effect = [{"status": "ok"}, TimeoutError("gateway down")]
print("first refund:", gateway.refund("ch_1"))
try:
    gateway.refund("ch_2")
except TimeoutError as exc:
    print("second refund raised:", exc)

# The trap: a bare MagicMock invents whatever you ask for, including your typos.
loose = MagicMock()
print("typo silently 'works':", bool(loose.chrage(1999)))

class Gateway:
    def charge(self, amount: int, currency: str) -> dict: ...

strict = create_autospec(Gateway, instance=True)
try:
    strict.chrage(1999)
except AttributeError as exc:
    print("autospec catches it:", exc)
try:
    strict.charge(1999)                      # missing a required argument
except TypeError as exc:
    print("autospec checks the signature:", exc)

returned: {'id': 'ch_1', 'status': 'succeeded'}
called once: True
call args: call(amount=1999, currency='eur')
first refund: {'status': 'ok'}
second refund raised: gateway down
typo silently 'works': True
autospec catches it: Mock object has no attribute 'chrage'
autospec checks the signature: missing a required argument: 'currency'

That contrast is the single most important thing to know about mock. A bare MagicMock cannot fail an assertion about a method that does not exist, so a suite full of them keeps passing after you rename the real method — the worst possible outcome, since it is green and wrong. create_autospec (or patch(..., autospec=True)) builds the double from the real object's signature, so a rename breaks the test the way it should.

Where to patch. patch replaces a name in a namespace, and the name that matters is the one the code under test looks up, not the one where the function is defined.

import sys, tempfile, pathlib, textwrap
from unittest.mock import patch

root = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(root / "clock.py").write_text("def now():\n    return 'REAL TIME'\n")
(root / "billing.py").write_text(textwrap.dedent("""
    from clock import now              # bound into billing's namespace at import time

    def stamp():
        return f"invoice at {now()}"
"""))
sys.path.insert(0, str(root))
import billing

print("unpatched:", billing.stamp())

with patch("clock.now", return_value="FAKE"):            # patches the wrong name
    print("patching clock.now:  ", billing.stamp())

with patch("billing.now", return_value="FAKE"):          # patches where it is used
    print("patching billing.now:", billing.stamp())

unpatched: invoice at REAL TIME
patching clock.now:   invoice at REAL TIME
patching billing.now: invoice at FAKE

from clock import now copied the function object into billing's globals when billing was imported (§11.1). Rebinding clock.now afterwards changes nothing that billing can see. Patch where it is used, not where it is defined — or write import clock and call clock.now(), which makes the lookup happen at call time and both patches work.

Use the least powerful double that answers the question. In order: a real object; a simple fake you wrote (a dict-backed repository, an in-memory queue); monkeypatch; create_autospec; a bare MagicMock. Every step up buys convenience and pays in tests that pass when the code is broken. And do not mock what you do not own — wrap the third-party client in your own thin interface and fake that, so a change in their API breaks one adapter test instead of forty.

12.7 Exceptions, Warnings, and Async Tests

import pytest, warnings

def test_raises_with_message():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match=r"quantity must not be negative") as exc_info:
        line_total(10.0, -1)
    assert exc_info.value.args[0].startswith("quantity")

def test_exception_group():                       # §7.6
    with pytest.raises(ExceptionGroup) as exc_info:
        raise ExceptionGroup("boom", [ValueError("a"), KeyError("b")])
    assert len(exc_info.value.exceptions) == 2

def test_warns():
    with pytest.warns(DeprecationWarning, match="use line_total"):
        old_total(10.0, 3)

def test_no_warning():
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("error")
        line_total(10.0, 3)

match is a regular expression searched against str(exception), and it is not optional discipline — pytest.raises(ValueError) alone passes when the function raised the wrong ValueError, which is a real way to write a test that never fails.

pytest.approx is the other half of this pair, for the float comparisons §12.5 just demonstrated:

assert 0.1 + 0.2 == pytest.approx(0.3)
assert [0.1 + 0.2, 1.0] == pytest.approx([0.3, 1.0])
assert 29.985 == pytest.approx(29.99, abs=0.01)

Async tests need a plugin, because a coroutine function returns a coroutine and pytest cannot await it. Two exist: pytest-asyncio and anyio's plugin (which also runs the test on Trio).

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
asyncio_mode = "auto"        # pytest-asyncio: no decorator needed on async tests

import asyncio
import pytest

@pytest.mark.asyncio                       # unnecessary in "auto" mode
async def test_gather_runs_concurrently():
    async def work(n):
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
        return n * 2
    assert await asyncio.gather(*(work(i) for i in range(3))) == [0, 2, 4]

@pytest.fixture
async def client():                        # async fixtures work the same way
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    yield {"ready": True}

Two rules specific to async tests. Never assert on wall-clock durations to prove concurrency — that is a flaky test on a loaded CI machine; assert on ordering or on the number of concurrent entries instead. And give every awaited network call a timeout in the test (asyncio.timeout, §9.6), because a hung coroutine otherwise stalls the suite until CI kills the job.

12.8 The Built-in Fixtures

pytest ships a set of fixtures that cover most of what tests need from the outside world. Using them instead of hand-rolled equivalents is what keeps tests independent.

import logging, sys
import pytest

def test_tmp_path(tmp_path):                       # a fresh directory, auto-removed
    target = tmp_path / "notes.txt"
    target.write_text("hello\n", encoding="utf-8")
    assert target.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip() == "hello"

def test_capsys(capsys):                           # captured stdout/stderr
    print("shipped 3 orders")
    out, err = capsys.readouterr()
    assert "3 orders" in out

def test_caplog(caplog):                           # captured log records (§7.8)
    with caplog.at_level(logging.WARNING, logger="cart"):
        logging.getLogger("cart").warning("stock low: %s", "SKU-9")
    assert caplog.records[0].levelname == "WARNING"
    assert "SKU-9" in caplog.text

def test_monkeypatch(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv("CART_ENV", "test")
    monkeypatch.setattr(sys, "maxsize", 99)        # restored automatically afterwards
    assert sys.maxsize == 99

@pytest.mark.skipif(sys.platform == "win32", reason="POSIX only")
def test_skipped_elsewhere():
    assert True

@pytest.mark.xfail(reason="rounding bug, tracked in #412", strict=True)
def test_known_bug():
    assert 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3

$ pytest -q
.....x                                                                   [100%]
=========================== short test summary info ============================
XFAIL tests/test_builtin.py::test_known_bug - rounding bug, tracked in #412
5 passed, 1 xfailed in 0.06s

caplog.records gives you the LogRecord objects themselves, so you can assert on levelname, name and the structured extra fields rather than on formatted text — the right way to test the logging from §7.8.

xfail with strict=True is the useful form: the test is expected to fail, and if it starts passing the suite fails, telling you the bug is fixed and the marker should go. Non-strict xfail silently accepts either outcome, which makes it a way to forget about a bug forever. skip and skipif mean "this cannot run here" — a missing optional dependency, the wrong platform. Neither is a place to park a broken test; a reason linking an issue is the minimum.

Also available: tmp_path_factory (session-scoped temp dirs), capfd (captures at file-descriptor level, so it catches output from subprocesses and C libraries that capsys misses), recwarn, and request for introspecting the running test.

12.9 Coverage — and What It Does Not Measure

coverage.py records which lines ran. pytest-cov wires it into pytest.

[tool.coverage.run]
branch = true                 # measure branches, not just lines
source = ["src"]

[tool.coverage.report]
show_missing = true
skip_covered = true
fail_under = 90

$ coverage run -m pytest -q && coverage report
Name                  Stmts   Miss Branch BrPart  Cover   Missing
-----------------------------------------------------------------
src/cart/pricing.py       6      2      4      2    60%   3, 5
-----------------------------------------------------------------
TOTAL                     6      2      4      2    60%

1 file skipped due to complete coverage.
Coverage failure: total of 60 is less than fail-under=90

branch = true is the setting that makes the number mean something. Without it, an if whose body always runs counts as fully covered even though the "skip it" path has never executed once. With it, BrPart counts branches taken only one way, and the Missing column names them.

coverage html writes a browsable report where every uncovered line is highlighted — far more useful than the percentage for actually finding untested code.

What coverage does not tell you. It measures execution, not verification. A test that calls every function and asserts nothing scores 100%. It cannot see a missing test for an input you never thought of, and it says nothing about whether the assertions are right. High coverage is weak evidence of a good suite; low coverage is strong evidence of a bad one. That asymmetry is the whole story.

Which is why a fail_under gate belongs at a level you can honestly hold — 80–90% for most code — and why chasing 100% produces tests written to satisfy the tool. Use # pragma: no cover sparingly and only for genuinely unreachable code (a if TYPE_CHECKING: block, a defensive raise AssertionError("unreachable")).

If you want a check on assertion quality, that is mutation testing: mutmut or cosmic-ray change a > to a >=, re-run the suite, and report every mutation that no test caught. It is slow enough to run nightly rather than per-commit, and it is the only automated answer to "are these assertions doing anything".

12.10 Property-Based Testing with Hypothesis

Example-based tests check the cases you thought of. Hypothesis generates hundreds of cases you did not, and when one fails it shrinks it to the smallest input that still fails.

from hypothesis import given, strategies as st
from cart.text import normalise           # " ".join(s.split()).lower()

@given(st.text())
def test_normalise_is_idempotent(s):
    assert normalise(normalise(s)) == normalise(s)

@given(st.text())
def test_normalise_never_has_double_spaces(s):
    assert "  " not in normalise(s)

Those are properties: statements true for every input, not for one. The four shapes that cover most real uses:

Property Shape Example
Round-trip decode(encode(x)) == x serialisers, parsers, compression
Invariant f(x) always satisfies P output is sorted; total is never negative
Idempotence f(f(x)) == f(x) normalisation, deduplication, abs
Oracle fast(x) == obvious(x) an optimisation against the naive version

Here is the payoff — the same function with a real bug, and what Hypothesis does with it:

# src/cart/report.py
def summarise(prices):
    return f"{len(prices)} items, average {sum(prices) // len(prices)}"

# tests/test_props.py
@given(st.lists(st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=10_000)))
def test_summarise_returns_a_string(prices):
    assert isinstance(summarise(prices), str)

$ pytest -q
    def summarise(prices):
>       return f"{len(prices)} items, average {sum(prices) // len(prices)}"
                                               ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
E       ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
E       Failing test case: test_summarise_returns_a_string(
E           prices=[],
E       )

1 failed in 0.44s

prices=[] is the shrunk result, not the input that first failed — Hypothesis found a failure with some random list, then reduced it repeatedly until nothing smaller failed. The reported counterexample is always the minimal one, which is why the failures are readable.

Two mechanisms make it usable in CI. Hypothesis keeps a .hypothesis/ database of previously failing examples and replays them first on the next run, so a fixed bug stays fixed deterministically — commit the directory or cache it in CI. And @example(...) pins a specific case permanently alongside the generated ones:

from hypothesis import given, example, settings, strategies as st

@given(st.lists(st.integers()))
@example([])                                   # the regression, forever
@settings(max_examples=500, deadline=None)     # deadline=None for slow code
def test_summarise(prices):
    ...

Strategies compose, which is what makes it applicable to real domain objects rather than just integers:

orders = st.builds(
    Order,
    id=st.uuids(),
    quantity=st.integers(min_value=1, max_value=100),
    price=st.decimals(min_value=0, max_value=10_000, places=2),
    tags=st.lists(st.text(min_size=1), max_size=5, unique=True),
)

@given(orders)
def test_total_is_never_negative(order):
    assert order.total() >= 0

Use property tests where the properties are real: parsers, serialisers, anything with an inverse, ordering and dedup logic, and arithmetic on money. Do not force them on code whose only property is "it returns what the spec says", where a parametrised table is clearer and faster.

12.11 ruff: Linting and Formatting

ruff is a linter and formatter that replaces flake8, isort, pyupgrade, pydocstyle, bandit's common rules and black, running fast enough to be imperceptible on save.

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100
target-version = "py311"

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B", "SIM", "C4", "RUF"]
ignore = ["E501"]                       # the formatter owns line length

[tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores]
"tests/**" = ["S101"]                   # asserts are the point in tests

import os
import json
from typing import List


def load(path, keys = []):
    f = open(path)
    data = json.load(f)
    result: List[str] = []
    for k in keys:
        if k in data.keys():
            result.append(str(data[k]))
    return result

$ ruff check --output-format=concise .
messy.py:1:1: I001 [*] Import block is un-sorted or un-formatted
messy.py:1:8: F401 [*] `os` imported but unused
messy.py:3:1: UP035 `typing.List` is deprecated, use `list` instead
messy.py:6:23: B006 Do not use mutable data structures for argument defaults
messy.py:7:9: SIM115 Use a context manager for opening files
messy.py:9:13: UP006 [*] Use `list` instead of `List` for type annotation
messy.py:11:12: SIM118 Use `key in dict` instead of `key in dict.keys()`
Found 7 errors.
[*] 3 fixable with the `--fix` option (2 hidden fixes can be enabled with the `--unsafe-fixes` option).

Every one of those is a real defect or a real modernisation, and B006 — the mutable default argument of §1.2 — is a genuine bug the linter caught for free. Note the [*] markers: ruff check --fix applies those automatically, and the two "hidden" fixes are held back because they could change behaviour (deleting an import might remove a side effect).

The rule families worth enabling on a new project: E/W (pycodestyle), F (pyflakes — real errors), I (import sorting), UP (pyupgrade — modernise for your target-version), B (bugbear — likely bugs), SIM (simplifications), C4 (comprehensions), RUF (ruff's own), and S (bandit security rules) on anything handling untrusted input. Add ANN if you want annotations enforced, and D for docstrings, but adopt them on a new codebase rather than retrofitting them onto a large one in a single commit.

ruff check .                 # lint
ruff check --fix .           # lint and autofix
ruff format .                # format
ruff format --diff .         # what would change, without changing it
ruff check --statistics .    # a histogram: what to fix first on a legacy codebase
