2026-08  65.49   7.25
2026-09  99.00  12.00

The operations that cover most work: read_csv/read_parquet/read_sql to load; df[mask] with boolean conditions to filter (& and |, with parentheses — and and or do not work on Series); df.loc[rows, cols] for label-based selection and df.iloc for positional; groupby(...).agg(...); merge for joins; pivot_table for cross-tabs; assign to add columns without mutating; dropna/fillna for missing data; and .dt/.str accessors for datetime and string operations on a whole column.

Two things in that output are worth noting because they are recent. The customer column has dtype str, not object — pandas 3.0 made a proper string dtype the default, which is faster and no longer silently accepts mixed types. And datetime64[us] shows that pandas now preserves the resolution the data implies rather than forcing nanoseconds. Code written against pandas 1.x may assume object and datetime64[ns].

Two habits prevent most pandas pain. Chain, do not mutate — df.assign(...).query(...).groupby(...) is easier to reason about than a sequence of in-place edits, and pandas 3.0's copy-on-write makes the old SettingWithCopyWarning dance obsolete. And never iterate rows with iterrows(); it is slow and it loses dtypes. If you cannot express something as a vectorised operation or a groupby, apply is the escape hatch, and it is still a Python-level loop.

polars is worth knowing about as the modern alternative: a different API built on Arrow, with lazy evaluation and multi-threaded execution, typically several times faster on large frames. For work at a scale where pandas struggles it is the first thing to try, and its expression API is closer to SQL than to pandas.

13.12 Choosing a Dependency

You will make this decision constantly, and the cost of a bad one is measured in years.

Is it in the standard library? Check first. It is already installed, already audited, and it will still work in ten years.
Is it maintained? Recent releases, issues answered, more than one maintainer, and a stated support policy for Python versions.
What does it drag in? pip download or uv tree shows the transitive set. Forty packages for one function is forty things that can break.
Does it ship types and wheels? A py.typed marker and a wheel for your platform mean it will work with your checker and install without a compiler.
Could you replace it? A dependency behind your own thin interface can be swapped. One whose types are threaded through your domain model cannot.

Two security habits belong here rather than in a separate chapter. Typosquatting is real: python -m pip install requets installs whatever someone registered under that name, and it runs at install time. Read the name you typed. And pin with hashes for anything deployed (§11.11) so the artefact you tested is the artefact that runs. pip-audit checks an environment against the advisory database and belongs in CI, next to the tests.

Exercises

Exercise 13.1 — Replace the dependencies. This script's imports include three things the standard library already does. Rewrite it, and say what each replacement gains.

import os
import requests
import yaml
from dateutil.parser import parse as parse_date

config = yaml.load(open("config.yaml"))
outdir = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "reports", config["name"])
os.makedirs(outdir, exist_ok=True)
cutoff = parse_date(config["cutoff"])
Solution 
import tomllib
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

with open(Path(__file__).parent / "config.toml", "rb") as fh:   # tomllib needs binary
    config = tomllib.load(fh)

outdir = Path(__file__).parent / "reports" / config["name"]
outdir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
cutoff = datetime.fromisoformat(config["cutoff"])

yaml → tomllib. TOML is in the standard library from 3.11 and gives real types, so cutoff could be a native datetime in the file itself. If the file must stay YAML, the minimum change is yaml.safe_load — the original yaml.load without a Loader constructs arbitrary Python objects and is a code-execution hole. Note also the original leaks a file handle; tomllib.load here is inside a with.

os.path → pathlib. One expression instead of three functions, and mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) replaces makedirs.

dateutil → datetime.fromisoformat. Since 3.11 it parses the full ISO 8601 range, which is what a config file should contain. dateutil is still the right answer for parsing unpredictable human-written dates — that is a different problem.

requests is not replaced — and that is the point of the exercise. urllib.request exists, but it is unpleasant enough that requests or httpx earns its place. Knowing which dependencies are worth it matters more than minimising the count; httpx is the modern choice because it also does async and HTTP/2 with the same API.

Exercise 13.2 — Find four bugs. This endpoint has four defects: one security, one correctness, one durability, one design.

@app.post("/orders")
async def create_order(request: Request):
    data = json.loads(await request.body())
    con = sqlite3.connect("orders.db")
    con.execute(
        f"INSERT INTO orders (customer, total) VALUES ('{data['customer']}', {data['total']})"
    )
    con.close()
    return {"status": "created", "customer": data["customer"]}
Solution

Security — SQL injection. data['customer'] is formatted straight into the statement, so a customer name of x'); DROP TABLE orders; -- executes. Use ? placeholders. This is not mitigated by validating elsewhere; parameterisation is the fix.

Correctness — no validation at all. A missing total raises KeyError and returns a 500; a total of "abc" or -100 is accepted. Take a pydantic model as the parameter and let FastAPI reject bad input with a 422 (§13.9). That also removes the manual json.loads.

Durability — nothing is committed. sqlite3 opens a transaction implicitly and con.close() discards it, so every order is silently lost while the endpoint returns 201. Use with con:. A connection per request is the second half of this problem: opening the database on every request is slow and, under an async server, blocks the event loop.

Design — a blocking driver in an async def handler. sqlite3 is synchronous, so every request stalls the loop and the server's concurrency collapses under load (§9.11). Either make the handler def — FastAPI runs it in a thread pool — or use an async driver such as aiosqlite.

class OrderIn(BaseModel):
    customer: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=100)
    total: int = Field(ge=0)                       # integer cents

@app.post("/orders", status_code=201)
def create_order(order: OrderIn, db: Annotated[sqlite3.Connection, Depends(get_db)]):
    with db:
        cur = db.execute("INSERT INTO orders (customer, total) VALUES (?, ?)",
                         (order.customer, order.total))
    return {"id": cur.lastrowid, "customer": order.customer}

Note the handler is now def, the connection arrives from a dependency (so tests can override it), and the response includes the id — the original told the client nothing it could use.

Exercise 13.3 — Which tool? For each task, choose between the standard library, NumPy, pandas, and a database, and justify it.

  1. Average of 40 numbers in a CLI tool.
  2. Count occurrences of each error code in a 3 GB log file.
  3. Element-wise arithmetic on a 10-million-row numeric column.
  4. Joining two CSV files on a key and grouping the result.
  5. Storing a desktop application's user data, queried in several ways.
Solution

1. statistics.fmean. Adding NumPy to a CLI for this costs ~20 MB and a second of import time to save one line. fmean is faster than mean and returns a float.

2. collections.Counter over a generator. The file does not fit comfortably in memory, and the operation is one streaming pass:

counts = Counter(m.group(1) for line in path.open(encoding="utf-8")
                 if (m := ERROR_RE.search(line)))

Reading a 3 GB file into a DataFrame to count a column is the wrong shape of solution — and if you need pandas anyway, read_csv(..., chunksize=...) streams.

3. NumPy. This is exactly what it is for: one dtype, one contiguous block, whole-array arithmetic in compiled code. pandas would also work — it is NumPy underneath — but the labels and index cost memory you have no use for.

4. pandas. A join plus a group-by on labelled columns is its core competence, and merge handles the join semantics you would otherwise write by hand. If the files are large enough to be slow, polars or loading both into SQLite and writing a JOIN are both reasonable.

5. SQLite. Multiple query shapes over persistent structured data is the definition of a database. A JSON file rewritten on every change loses data on a crash, cannot be queried without loading all of it, and has no transactions. sqlite3 costs no dependency and no server.

The pattern: match the tool to the data's shape and size, not to its familiarity. The most common real error is the last one — reaching for pandas because it is known, when the data is a stream (2) or a store (5) rather than a table.

Exercise 13.4 — Draw the boundary. A service reads a JSON message from a queue, writes a row to PostgreSQL, and calls a third-party API. Say where validation happens, which types cross which boundary, and what pickle should be allowed to touch.

Solution

Validate once, at each edge, immediately on arrival.

queue message (bytes) — untrusted
json.loads → dict → Message.model_validate(...)
the only place raw input is trusted
↓
domain object (dataclass) — validated
the core works only with these, and imports no validation library
repository.save(order)
parameterised SQL, no dicts; schema constraints as the last line of defence
gateway.charge(order)
its own request model — and the response is validated too

Three boundaries, three validations. The queue message is untrusted and gets a pydantic model. The third-party API's response is also untrusted — it is someone else's code, it changes without notice, and validating it turns "a field went missing" into a clear error at the boundary instead of an AttributeError three layers deep. The database is trusted for shape (the schema enforces it) but its constraints (NOT NULL, CHECK, foreign keys) are the last line of defence, and should exist even though the application validates first.

Types across the boundaries. Bytes in, pydantic model at the edge, then convert to plain dataclasses for the core (§13.7). The core should not import pydantic: it makes the domain logic testable without constructing validated models, and it means a change of validation library does not reach into your business rules. Going out, convert domain objects to the request model the gateway needs.

pickle touches none of it. Nothing here is inside a single trust boundary: a queue is written by other services, a database can be written by other applications, and a third-party API is by definition foreign. Use JSON on the wire, real columns in the database, and reserve pickle for multiprocessing and a local cache you alone write and read.

The reason this shape is worth the ceremony: every one of these boundaries will eventually deliver something you did not expect, and the difference between a clear rejection at the edge and a corrupt row written at 3 a.m. is exactly where the validation sits.

SECTION 14

Capstone Project: Sentinel, an Async Service Monitor

Everything in this course exists in this project. Sentinel is a service health monitor: it reads a TOML file describing services, checks them all concurrently, records the results in SQLite, prints a report, and exits with a status code CI can act on. It uses no third-party libraries at all — the standard library is enough, and building it that way is the point.

This section is a project brief with a worked solution. Build it yourself first, from the requirements and the build order. Read the solution when you are finished, or when you are properly stuck — comparing your design to another one is where most of the value is.

14.1 What You Are Building

$ sentinel check --config services.toml
OK   api          12.4 ms  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
OK   cache         0.8 ms  connected
SLOW reports      54.1 ms  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
DOWN billing       3.2 ms  billing: HTTP 503
DOWN legacy      201.7 ms  timed out
2 of 5 down
$ echo $?
1

The requirements, in full:

  1. Configuration is a TOML file with a [target.<name>] table per service: host, port, an optional path (present means "speak HTTP", absent means "just open a TCP connection"), an optional timeout and an optional slow_after_ms. A malformed config fails at startup with a message naming the offending target.
  2. Checks run concurrently, with a configurable ceiling on how many run at once.
  3. Every check has a deadline. A target that never answers must not stall the run.
  4. A transient failure is retried with exponential backoff before being called down.
  5. Results are stored in SQLite with a timestamp, so sentinel history and an uptime percentage per target are available later.
  6. The report is sorted with failures first, and the process exits 0 when everything is up and 1 otherwise.
  7. Errors are the program's own types, not raw OSErrors escaping to the top level.
  8. It is a package: pip install -e . gives you a sentinel command.
  9. It is tested without a network, without sleep, and without mocking the thing under test.

14.2 Build Order

Build it bottom-up; each stage is runnable and testable before the next one exists.

1. Types first. Status, Target, CheckResult, and the exception hierarchy. Everything else is written against these.
2. Config parsing. TOML text → list[Target], raising ConfigError with a useful message. Testable with a string; no files needed.
3. One check. tcp_check against a server you start in the test. Then http_check.
4. The runner. Timeout, then retry, then concurrency, then the task group — in that order, so each behaviour is added to something that already works.
5. The store. Schema, insert, two queries. SQLite in memory in tests, a file in production.
6. The CLI and the packaging. Last, because everything under it is already proven.

14.3 The Hard Parts

Five decisions will take longer than the rest of the project put together. They are worth thinking about before you start.

Where does the timeout go? Inside the check, or around it? Around it — asyncio.timeout (§9.6) wrapping the whole check means a target with a slow DNS lookup, a slow connect and a slow response is still bounded by one number, and the check itself stays free of timing code. Note that the timeout must be inside the semaphore's async with or a target that waits for a slot will have its own deadline eaten by the queue.

How do concurrency and cancellation interact? TaskGroup (§9.5) cancels its siblings when a task raises. That is exactly what you do not want here: one unreachable host must not abort the run. So run_one catches its own failures and returns a CheckResult describing them — the task group only sees success. Letting an exception escape the task and then trying to reassemble the results from an ExceptionGroup is possible, and much worse.

What is a failure, and what is a result? A refused connection is a normal outcome of a monitoring tool — it is data, not an error. ConfigError is an error: the program cannot proceed. Draw that line deliberately (§7.2), because it decides which layer each try belongs in.

How do you test time-dependent behaviour without waiting? By making the durations parameters and choosing tiny ones. The retry backoff starts at 10 ms, so a three-attempt failure costs 30 ms; the "slow" threshold is per-target, so a test sets it to 10 ms and a 50 ms server is reliably slow. Never assert on an absolute duration (§12.7).

How do you test network code without a network? asyncio.start_server on port 0 gives you a real server on a real socket on a port the OS picks — no mocks, no fixed ports, no collisions under pytest -n auto, and the code under test is exercised for real. This is the single most useful technique in the project.

14.4 Types and Errors

import asyncio
import functools
import logging
import sqlite3
import time
import tomllib
from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable, Iterable, Iterator
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from enum import StrEnum
from typing import Protocol, Self

log = logging.getLogger("sentinel")


class SentinelError(Exception):
    """Base class for every error this package raises deliberately."""


class ConfigError(SentinelError):
    """The configuration is unusable; the program cannot start."""


class CheckFailed(SentinelError):
    """A target answered, but not acceptably."""

    def __init__(self, target: str, reason: str) -> None:
        super().__init__(f"{target}: {reason}")
        self.target = target
        self.reason = reason


class Status(StrEnum):
    UP = "up"
    DOWN = "down"
    SLOW = "slow"


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Target:
    name: str
    host: str
    port: int
    path: str | None = None
    timeout: float = 2.0
    slow_after_ms: float = 500.0

    @classmethod
    def from_toml(cls, name: str, raw: dict[str, object]) -> Self:
        def need(key: str) -> object:
            if key not in raw:
                raise ConfigError(f"target {name!r} is missing {key!r}")
            return raw[key]

        try:
            return cls(
                name=name,
                host=str(need("host")),
                port=int(str(need("port"))),          # str() first: raw is dict[str, object]
                path=str(raw["path"]) if "path" in raw else None,
                timeout=float(str(raw.get("timeout", 2.0))),
                slow_after_ms=float(str(raw.get("slow_after_ms", 500.0))),
            )
        except (TypeError, ValueError) as exc:
            raise ConfigError(f"target {name!r}: {exc}") from exc


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class CheckResult:
    target: str
    status: Status
    elapsed_ms: float
    detail: str = ""
    at: datetime = field(default_factory=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc))

    @property
    def ok(self) -> bool:
        return self.status is not Status.DOWN

Four choices in there are the ones a reviewer would ask about.

frozen=True, slots=True (§3.9): a Target is a value read from configuration and a CheckResult is a record of something that happened — neither should ever be mutated, and slots removes the per-instance __dict__ for objects you may have thousands of.

A three-member StrEnum, not a boolean (§3.10). "Slow" is a real state that a boolean cannot express, and StrEnum means str(status) is "up", so it goes into SQLite and out of a JSON encoder unchanged.

from_toml translates every failure into ConfigError (§7.4), so a caller has one exception type to handle. The str() around each value is not decoration: tomllib returns dict[str, object], and int(some_object) does not type-check — going through str makes the conversion honest, and int("no") still raises the ValueError that becomes the message target 'a': invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'no'.

default_factory for at (§3.9): a mutable or "computed now" default must not be evaluated once at class-definition time, which is what a plain default would do — the same bug as §1.2's mutable default argument.

14.5 Checks

class Check(Protocol):
    async def __call__(self, target: Target) -> str: ...


async def tcp_check(target: Target) -> str:
    reader, writer = await asyncio.open_connection(target.host, target.port)
    writer.close()
    await writer.wait_closed()
    return "connected"


async def http_check(target: Target) -> str:
    reader, writer = await asyncio.open_connection(target.host, target.port)
    try:
        request = (
            f"GET {target.path} HTTP/1.1\r\n"
            f"Host: {target.host}\r\n"
            "Connection: close\r\n\r\n"
        )
        writer.write(request.encode("ascii"))
        await writer.drain()
        status_line = (await reader.readline()).decode("ascii", "replace").strip()
        if not status_line.startswith("HTTP/"):
            raise CheckFailed(target.name, f"not an HTTP response: {status_line!r}")
        code = int(status_line.split(" ")[1])
        if code >= 400:
            raise CheckFailed(target.name, f"HTTP {code}")
        return status_line
    finally:
        writer.close()
        await writer.wait_closed()


def pick_check(target: Target) -> Check:
    return http_check if target.path is not None else tcp_check

Check is a Protocol (§6.6), so a check is any async callable with that signature. Nothing inherits from it, and a test can pass a plain async def that returns a canned string. That is structural typing doing real work: the runner depends on a shape, not on a class hierarchy.

The try/finally around the HTTP exchange is not decoration. Without it, a CheckFailed raised on a 503 leaks the socket, and after a few hundred checks the process runs out of file descriptors — the kind of bug that only appears in production, on the third day.

14.6 Retry and the Runner

def retry[**P, R](
    attempts: int = 3, base_delay: float = 0.01
) -> Callable[[Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]], Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]]:
    """Retry a coroutine function on transient network errors, with backoff."""
    def decorate(fn: Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]) -> Callable[P, Awaitable[R]]:
        @functools.wraps(fn)
        async def wrapper(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
            last: Exception | None = None
            for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1):
                try:
                    return await fn(*args, **kwargs)
                except (OSError, TimeoutError) as exc:
                    last = exc
                    log.debug("attempt %d/%d failed: %s", attempt, attempts, exc)
                    if attempt < attempts:
                        await asyncio.sleep(base_delay * 2 ** (attempt - 1))
            assert last is not None
            raise last
        return wrapper
    return decorate


async def run_one(target: Target, sem: asyncio.Semaphore) -> CheckResult:
    check = retry()(pick_check(target))
    started = time.perf_counter()
    async with sem:                                  # bound concurrency
        try:
            async with asyncio.timeout(target.timeout):    # bound total time
                detail = await check(target)
        except TimeoutError:
            return CheckResult(target.name, Status.DOWN,
                               (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000, "timed out")
        except (OSError, CheckFailed) as exc:
            return CheckResult(target.name, Status.DOWN,
                               (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000, str(exc))
    elapsed = (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000
    status = Status.SLOW if elapsed > target.slow_after_ms else Status.UP
    return CheckResult(target.name, status, elapsed, detail)


async def run_all(targets: Iterable[Target], concurrency: int = 10) -> list[CheckResult]:
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency)
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tasks = [tg.create_task(run_one(t, sem), name=t.name) for t in targets]
    return [t.result() for t in tasks]

This is the heart of the program, and every line is a decision from §8 and §9.

retry()(pick_check(target)) applies a decorator at runtime rather than with @ syntax, because which function is being decorated depends on the target. A decorator is just a function that takes a function (§4.4); @ is sugar for exactly this call.

The decorator is generic in both directions — [**P, R] (§6.10) says it preserves whatever parameters and return type the wrapped coroutine had. Without that, retry returns Callable[..., Any] and every caller silently loses its types; mypy --strict rejects the untyped version outright, which is how this one came to be written that way.

CheckFailed is deliberately not retried. A 503 is an answer, and retrying it three times turns a monitoring tool into a small denial-of-service. Only OSError and TimeoutError — genuinely transient conditions — are.

asyncio.sleep for backoff, never time.sleep (§9.11). time.sleep would block the event loop and stall every other check in flight.

The semaphore is outside the timeout. Reversed, a target queuing behind nine others would spend its deadline waiting for a slot and time out without a single packet being sent.

run_one never raises. That is what keeps TaskGroup from cancelling the other checks when one host is unreachable, and it is why the return type is a CheckResult describing a failure rather than an exception.

t.result() after the async with is safe because the task group has already awaited every task. Reading .result() on a task that has not finished raises InvalidStateError.

14.7 Store and Report

SCHEMA = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS result (
    id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    target  TEXT    NOT NULL,
    status  TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('up', 'down', 'slow')),
    ms      REAL    NOT NULL CHECK (ms >= 0),
    detail  TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    at      TEXT    NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS result_target_at ON result (target, at);
"""


class Store:
    def __init__(self, path: str) -> None:
        self.con = sqlite3.connect(path)
        self.con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        self.con.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
        self.con.executescript(SCHEMA)

    def __enter__(self) -> Self:
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *exc_info: object) -> None:
        self.con.close()

    def save(self, results: Iterable[CheckResult]) -> int:
        rows = [(r.target, str(r.status), r.elapsed_ms, r.detail, r.at.isoformat())
                for r in results]
        with self.con:                                    # transaction, not close
            cur = self.con.executemany(
                "INSERT INTO result (target, status, ms, detail, at) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)",
                rows,
            )
        return cur.rowcount

    def history(self, target: str, limit: int = 10) -> list[sqlite3.Row]:
        return self.con.execute(
            "SELECT status, ms, at FROM result WHERE target = ? ORDER BY at DESC LIMIT ?",
            (target, limit),
        ).fetchall()

    def uptime(self) -> dict[str, float]:
        rows = self.con.execute(
            "SELECT target, "
            "       SUM(CASE WHEN status != 'down' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS up "
            "FROM result GROUP BY target"
        ).fetchall()
        return {r["target"]: round(r["up"] * 100, 1) for r in rows}


def format_results(results: Iterable[CheckResult]) -> Iterator[str]:
    symbols = {Status.UP: "OK  ", Status.SLOW: "SLOW", Status.DOWN: "DOWN"}
    for r in sorted(results, key=lambda r: (r.status is not Status.DOWN, r.target)):
        yield f"{symbols[r.status]} {r.target:<12} {r.elapsed_ms:6.1f} ms  {r.detail}"


def exit_code(results: Iterable[CheckResult]) -> int:
    return 0 if all(r.ok for r in results) else 1


def load_targets(text: str) -> list[Target]:
    try:
        raw = tomllib.loads(text)
    except tomllib.TOMLDecodeError as exc:
        raise ConfigError(f"invalid TOML: {exc}") from exc
    targets = raw.get("target")
    if not isinstance(targets, dict) or not targets:
        raise ConfigError("no [target.*] tables found")
    return [Target.from_toml(name, body) for name, body in targets.items()]

Store is a context manager (§2.9) because a connection is a resource, and __exit__ accepting *exc_info closes it whether the body succeeded or raised. Note that with self.con: inside save is a transaction, not a close (§13.6) — the two with statements do entirely different things and both are needed.

The aggregation is SQL, not Python. uptime() could have pulled every row and counted in a comprehension; letting SQLite do it means the work happens where the index is and the memory cost does not grow with history.

format_results is a generator (§5.3), so the CLI can stream it to stdout, a test can take next() of it, and nothing builds a list that is immediately thrown away. The sort key (r.status is not Status.DOWN, r.target) puts failures first because False sorts before True — a small idiom worth recognising.

14.8 Proving It Works

The demo starts three real servers on OS-assigned ports, points the monitor at them plus one address that is guaranteed to refuse, and checks all five concurrently. No mocks anywhere.

async def fake_service(status_line: bytes, delay: float = 0.0):
    """A minimal HTTP server, used here and in the tests."""
    async def handle(reader, writer):
        await reader.readline()
        if delay:
            await asyncio.sleep(delay)
        writer.write(status_line + b"\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\nhi")
        await writer.drain()
        writer.close()
    server = await asyncio.start_server(handle, "127.0.0.1", 0)   # port 0: OS picks
    return server, server.sockets[0].getsockname()[1]


async def main() -> None:
    good, p_good = await fake_service(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK")
    bad,  p_bad  = await fake_service(b"HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable")
    slow, p_slow = await fake_service(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK", delay=0.05)

    targets = load_targets(f"""
        [target.api]
        host = "127.0.0.1"
        port = {p_good}
        path = "/health"

        [target.billing]
        host = "127.0.0.1"
        port = {p_bad}
        path = "/health"

        [target.reports]
        host = "127.0.0.1"
        port = {p_slow}
        path = "/health"
        slow_after_ms = 10

        [target.cache]
        host = "127.0.0.1"
        port = {p_good}

        [target.legacy]
        host = "127.0.0.1"
        port = 1
        timeout = 0.2
    """)

    results = await run_all(targets, concurrency=4)
    for r in sorted(results, key=lambda r: r.target):
        detail = "connection refused" if "Errno" in r.detail else r.detail
        print(f"{r.target:<8} {r.status.value:<4} {detail}")
    print("exit code:", exit_code(results))

    with Store(":memory:") as store:
        store.save(results)
        store.save(results)                       # a second round, same outcomes
        print("uptime %:", store.uptime())
        print("history rows for billing:", len(store.history("billing")))

    for s in (good, bad, slow):
        s.close()
        await s.wait_closed()

asyncio.run(main())

api      up   HTTP/1.1 200 OK
billing  down billing: HTTP 503
cache    up   connected
legacy   down connection refused
reports  slow HTTP/1.1 200 OK
exit code: 1
uptime %: {'api': 100.0, 'billing': 0.0, 'cache': 100.0, 'legacy': 0.0, 'reports': 100.0}
history rows for billing: 2

Five targets, four distinct outcomes, one run. cache has no path, so it took the TCP branch and reported connected; reports answered in 50 ms against a 10 ms threshold and came back slow; billing answered correctly with a 503 and is down without being retried; legacy was refused three times, with backoff, in well under its 200 ms deadline.

14.9 The Tests

import re

import pytest
from sentinel import (CheckResult, ConfigError, Status, Store, Target,
                      exit_code, load_targets, run_all)

from .conftest import fake_service          # the server helper from §14.8

@pytest.fixture
async def service():
    """Start a real server; yield its port; shut it down afterwards."""
    servers = []

    async def start(status_line=b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK", delay=0.0):
        server, port = await fake_service(status_line, delay)
        servers.append(server)
        return port

    yield start
    for server in servers:
        server.close()
        await server.wait_closed()


@pytest.mark.parametrize("toml_text, message", [
    ('[target.a]\nport = 80',              "missing 'host'"),
    ('[target.a]\nhost = "h"',             "missing 'port'"),
    ('[target.a]\nhost = "h"\nport = "no"', "invalid literal"),
    ('',                                   "no [target.*] tables"),
])
def test_config_errors_name_the_problem(toml_text, message):
    with pytest.raises(ConfigError, match=re.escape(message)):
        load_targets(toml_text)


async def test_http_503_is_down_and_not_retried(service):
    port = await service(b"HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable")
    target = Target("billing", "127.0.0.1", port, path="/health")
    [result] = await run_all([target])
    assert result.status is Status.DOWN
    assert "HTTP 503" in result.detail


async def test_slow_target_is_slow_not_down(service):
    port = await service(delay=0.05)
    target = Target("reports", "127.0.0.1", port, path="/", slow_after_ms=10)
    [result] = await run_all([target])
    assert result.status is Status.SLOW and result.ok


async def test_one_dead_target_does_not_cancel_the_others(service):
    port = await service()
    targets = [Target("good", "127.0.0.1", port, path="/"),
               Target("dead", "127.0.0.1", 1, timeout=0.2)]
    results = {r.target: r.status for r in await run_all(targets)}
    assert results == {"good": Status.UP, "dead": Status.DOWN}


def test_uptime_counts_slow_as_up():
    with Store(":memory:") as store:
        store.save([CheckResult("a", Status.UP, 1.0),
                    CheckResult("a", Status.SLOW, 900.0),
                    CheckResult("a", Status.DOWN, 5.0)])
        assert store.uptime() == {"a": 66.7}


def test_exit_code_is_one_when_anything_is_down():
    assert exit_code([CheckResult("a", Status.UP, 1.0)]) == 0
    assert exit_code([CheckResult("a", Status.UP, 1.0),
                      CheckResult("b", Status.DOWN, 1.0)]) == 1

Notice what is not here. Nothing is mocked — the HTTP tests speak to a real socket, and the store tests use a real database. There is no sleep and no assertion on a duration; "slow" is tested by setting the threshold to 10 ms rather than by making the test slow. And test_one_dead_target_does_not_cancel_the_others pins the single most subtle behaviour in the program, which is exactly the kind of thing that a refactor breaks silently.

The parametrised config test is the shape §12.5 argued for: four cases, four names in the output, and a failure tells you which malformed file stopped producing a good message.

14.10 Shipping It

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "sentinel-monitor"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Concurrent service health checks with history."
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
license = "MIT"
dependencies = []                       # the point: there are none

[dependency-groups]
dev = ["pytest>=8", "pytest-asyncio>=1.0", "ruff>=0.6", "mypy>=1.11"]

[project.scripts]
sentinel = "sentinel.cli:main"

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
asyncio_mode = "auto"
addopts = "-ra --strict-markers"

[tool.mypy]
strict = true

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B", "SIM", "RUF"]

The CLI is the last piece, and it is small because everything below it is finished:

def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="sentinel")
    parser.add_argument("--db", default="sentinel.db", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="count", default=0)
    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    check = sub.add_parser("check", help="check every target once")
    check.add_argument("--config", type=Path, required=True)
    check.add_argument("--concurrency", type=int, default=10)

    hist = sub.add_parser("history", help="recent results for one target")
    hist.add_argument("target")
    hist.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=10)
    return parser


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=[logging.WARNING, logging.INFO, logging.DEBUG][min(args.verbose, 2)],
        format="%(levelname)-8s %(name)s %(message)s",
    )
    try:
        with Store(str(args.db)) as store:
            if args.command == "check":
                targets = load_targets(args.config.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
                results = asyncio.run(run_all(targets, args.concurrency))
                store.save(results)
                for line in format_results(results):
                    print(line)
                down = sum(1 for r in results if not r.ok)
                print(f"{down} of {len(results)} down")
                return exit_code(results)
            for row in store.history(args.target, args.limit):
                print(f"{row['at']}  {row['status']:<4} {row['ms']:6.1f} ms")
            return 0
    except ConfigError as exc:
        print(f"sentinel: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    except FileNotFoundError as exc:
        print(f"sentinel: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

Three exit codes with three meanings: 0 everything up, 1 something is down, 2 the tool could not run at all. That distinction is what makes it usable from a shell script or a CI job, and it is why main catches ConfigError here rather than letting a traceback reach the user — an operator does not need your stack, they need the name of the target with the bad port.

14.11 What It Demonstrates

Section Where it appears
1–2 Object model, dunders frozen/slots dataclasses, StrEnum, __enter__/__exit__
3 Classes dataclasses, classmethod constructor, properties
4 Functions and decorators the retry decorator factory, functools.wraps
5 Iteration format_results as a generator; Store as a context manager (§2.9)
6 Typing Protocol for Check, Self, str \| None, strict mypy
7 Errors and logging the exception hierarchy, raise ... from, log.debug with %s
8–9 Concurrency TaskGroup, Semaphore, asyncio.timeout, cancellation discipline
11 Packaging pyproject.toml, src layout, a console-script entry point
12 Testing real servers instead of mocks, parametrisation, async fixtures
13 Ecosystem tomllib, sqlite3, pathlib, argparse — and no dependencies

14.12 Where to Take It

Each of these is a real extension, not busywork, and each one forces a design decision the current code does not have to make.

  • A watch subcommand that runs forever on an interval and handles SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly. You will need asyncio.get_running_loop().add_signal_handler and a cancellation path that still flushes the store.
  • Notifications on a state change rather than on every failure — which means reading the previous status out of the store and deciding what "flapping" means.
  • A plugin system for check types, using entry points (§11.13), so a separate package can add a redis_check without you editing Sentinel.
  • Percentile latency in the report: p50 and p95 per target from the history table. statistics.quantiles does it in Python; a window function does it in SQL. Try both and compare.
  • Property-based tests (§12.10) for load_targets: generate valid TOML from a strategy and assert it round-trips, then generate invalid TOML and assert it always raises ConfigError rather than anything else.
  • Structured logging with extra={"target": ..., "ms": ...} and a JSON formatter, so the output is queryable (§7.8).

You started this course able to write Python. You now understand why Python behaves the way it does — which is the difference between code that works and code you can be trusted with.

What you can now do

  1. Explain the language's behaviour from the object model. Names bind to objects, everything is an object, attribute lookup follows the MRO through descriptors, and almost every surprise in Python — mutable defaults, identity versus equality, why += on a tuple member both fails and succeeds — falls out of those rules rather than needing to be memorised.
  2. Design classes that fit the language. Dunder methods so your objects work with len, in, with, [] and the operators; dataclasses for records; __slots__ when there are a million of them; ABCs and protocols to state what you require.
  3. Use functions as the first-class values they are. Closures, decorators that preserve signatures, functools for caching and dispatch, and the knowledge of exactly when a default argument is evaluated.
  4. Write lazy pipelines. Generators, the iterator protocol, itertools, and context managers — processing a file larger than memory without thinking twice about it.
  5. Run a type checker in CI and mean it. Protocols, generics, variance, TypedDict, overloads, narrowing, and the judgement to know where annotations earn their keep and where they are noise.
  6. Handle failure deliberately. An exception hierarchy of your own, chaining that preserves the cause, exception groups, structured logging that is queryable, and a debugger you can attach to a running process.
  7. Choose the right concurrency for the workload. Threads, processes, free-threaded builds, subinterpreters and asyncio — and the ability to say which one a given bottleneck needs, and why the other three would not help.
  8. Write asyncio that does not fall over. Task groups, cancellation, timeouts, backpressure, and the discipline never to block the event loop.
  9. Make things faster on evidence. Profile before optimising, know that the answer is usually a data structure, and measure again afterwards.
  10. Ship it. An installable project with a lockfile, a test suite that fails when the code is wrong, a linter and a formatter that run automatically, and a package on PyPI with an entry point.

That is a working professional's toolkit. There is no part of a normal Python codebase you should now find opaque.

When Python surprises you

Most moments that stop an experienced developer are one of a handful of mechanisms, and you have seen all of them. Use this as a diagnostic list.

Symptom Where the answer is
"Why did my default argument keep its value from last time?" §1.2 — defaults are evaluated once, at definition
"Why is a is b False when a == b?" §1.4 — identity, equality, and interning
"Why does mutating one object change another?" §1.2 — names are bindings, not boxes
"Why did my __radd__ not fire?" §2.6 — reflected methods belong to the other operand
"Why is my class attribute shared between instances?" §3.1 — class body versus __init__
"Why did the subclass ignore my method?" §3.5 — MRO and C3 linearisation
"Why does my generator only work once?" §5.1 — an iterator is exhausted, not rewound
"Why does mypy reject a list[Dog] where list[Animal] is wanted?" §6.5 — invariance
"Why is my exception's cause missing?" §7.4 — raise ... from
"Why do my threads not go faster?" §8.2 — the GIL
"Why did my whole server stop while one request ran?" §9.11 — a blocking call on the event loop
"Why is this slow when it looks simple?" §10.5 — the complexity, not the constant factor
"Why does my import work here and not there?" §11.2 — sys.path and what is on it
"Why does my patched function not get called?" §12.6 — patch where it is used

Habits worth keeping

Run the code. Almost every claim about Python can be settled in a REPL in under ten seconds. This course was written that way, and doing so caught two dozen things that had felt obviously true — including the belief that four threads incrementing a counter reliably lose updates on 3.14, which they do not, and a frozen=True dataclass being hashable, which it is only if every field is.

Read the source. The standard library is Python you can open. inspect.getsource, or just following the traceback, answers more questions than searching does.

Prefer the boring construction. A dict, a list comprehension and a function beat a metaclass almost every time. The advanced machinery in this course exists so that you recognise it in other people's code and reach for it in the rare case that earns it.

Make the invalid state unrepresentable. A frozen dataclass, a StrEnum instead of a string, integer cents instead of a float, Literal instead of "one of these four strings" — each one moves a class of bug from runtime to the type checker, or eliminates it entirely.

Validate at the boundary, trust inside it. Everything that crosses into your program is untyped until you check it, and everything after that check should be a real object with a real type.

Leave the diagnostics behind. Structured logs, exception chaining, a test that reproduces the incident. The version of you that gets paged at 3 a.m. is a different person with much less context.

Where to go next

  • Read a real codebase. CPython's Lib/ is the obvious one; httpx, attrs, rich and pydantic are all readable, well tested and modern. Pick one, find an open issue labelled "good first issue", and write the patch.
  • Follow the language. Each release's What's New is short and worth the twenty minutes. PEPs are the reasoning behind the changes, and reading a few — 484, 492, 557, 634, 649, 703 — explains the shape of modern Python better than any summary.
  • Pick a depth. Async services and the web; data engineering with Arrow, Polars and Parquet; scientific computing with NumPy and JAX; or the interpreter itself — the free-threaded build and subinterpreters are the most interesting thing to happen to CPython in a decade, and both are young enough to contribute to.
  • Teach it. Explaining the descriptor protocol to someone else is how you find out whether you understand it.

Python rewards curiosity unusually well, because so little of it is hidden. When something surprises you, the mechanism is there to be found — and you now know where to look.
